after.title: Preprint: High-resolution spatiotemporal estimates of total and wildfire PM2.5 in the contiguous United States, 2018-2024: Implications for population exposure and mortality burden
after.authors: Liu, N.; Cheong, Y.; Larson, T.; Austin, E.; Seto, E.
after.abstract:
Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

data.label: Preprint: Patient, carer and clinical stakeholder views on using artificial intelligence and machine learning for the histopathological diagnosis of duodenal biopsies
data.summary: added: Preprint: Patient, carer and clinical stakeholder views on using artificial intelligence and machine learning for the histopathological diagnosis of duodenal biopsies

after.title: Preprint: Patient, carer and clinical stakeholder views on using artificial intelligence and machine learning for the histopathological diagnosis of duodenal biopsies
after.authors: Baby, J. G.; Jaeckle, F.; Williams, J.; Shepherd, K.; Urwin, H.; Soilleux, E. J.
after.abstract:
ObjectiveBiopsies are examined under the microscope by a pathologist, giving a diagnosis, which guides treatment and predicts prognosis. A shortage of pathologists and increasing workload leads to diagnostic delays, while for duodenal (small intestinal) biopsies, variable diagnostic concordance between pathologists limits accuracy. These challenges have motivated us to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated approach for the automated diagnosis of up to 80% of duodenal biopsies (i.e., most cases of the two most frequent diagnoses: coeliac disease and "normal"). We set out to understand patient, carer and stakeholder views regarding the adoption of such technology.

Methods and AnalysisWe conducted mixed-methods stakeholder engagement (February 2024 to June 2026). We ran a national online patients and carers questionnaire (n=231 respondents) and four UK focus-group workshops, one of which additionally captured Likert-scale attitudes1 immediately before and after a structured educational session (n=34 matched pairs). Healthcare professionals completed an online questionnaire (n=37) and took part in a structured workshop. Quantitative data were summarised descriptively; free-text and workshop data were analysed thematically and triangulated across all sources.

ResultsMost patients and carers supported AI-reliant diagnosis (68.4%) and would strongly trust systems with formal regulatory approval (66.7%). Most wanted to be informed if AI was used (73.6%), but only 52.4% felt explicit permission was necessary. Qualitative themes centred on clear and available evidence of accuracy, human oversight, transparent communication and clear terminology, with the term  machine learning being preferred to  artificial intelligence. Agreement ( agree or  strongly agree combined) with statements relating to trust, acceptance and perceived benefit of AI was significantly higher after a structured educational session (38.2% to 67.6%, 85.3% to 97.1%, and 52.9% to 97.1% respectively; all p[≤]0.003). Healthcare professionals favoured an AI  assistant model over full automation, citing the need for validation, explainability, data governance and workflow integration. Patients also preferred some level of human oversight.

ConclusionPatients and healthcare professionals are cautiously supportive of AI-assisted diagnosis of duodenal biopsies, conditional upon demonstration of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication. Attitudes towards AI-assisted diagnosis were more favourable after structured explanation.

Key MessagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSVery little is known about patients, carers or healthcare professionals views about the automation of diagnosis in pathology, using AI-based software solutions.

What this study adds{Rightarrow} This is the first study to investigate patient, carer and healthcare professional attitudes specifically to AI-mediated duodenal biopsy diagnosis. Around two-thirds of respondents supported AI-assisted diagnosis, contingent upon clear and available evidence of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication, together with appropriate regulatory approval of the technology.
{Rightarrow}Attitudes were markedly more favourable after a single structured educational session: agreement that AI could improve duodenal biopsy diagnosis nearly doubled and trust in healthcare AI rose substantially, suggesting that public views of AI in diagnosis can be influenced by clear explanation.
{Rightarrow}Patients and healthcare professionals both favour some ongoing level of human oversight of any AI-based diagnostic approach.


How this study might affect research, practice or policy{Rightarrow} Our study suggests that a phased, AI-assistant-first deployment model with defined validation and audit checkpoints would be most readily acceptable when introducing diagnostic AI into histopathology.
{Rightarrow}It indicates that appropriate information and education, for example, a patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) session, can increase trust in AI in healthcare.
{Rightarrow}It shows that patients and the public are more trusting of technology for which the term machine learning is used, rather than artificial intelligence (AI).
{Rightarrow}It offers a stakeholder-engagement template for use by others introducing AI-based diagnostics.

after.title: Preprint: MR-based normative volumetric analyses reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR-related craniosynostoses
after.authors: Delassus, O.; Sadoine, J.; Paternoster, G.; Chollet, L.; Ndambidi Yungi, B.; Beaufort, Q.; Taverne, M.; Boddaert, N.; Mangin, J.-F.; Khonsari, R. H.; Germanaud, D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Universite Paris-Saclay, CEA, Joliot Institute, NeuroSpin, UNIACT
after.abstract: Craniostenosis, a cranial malformation due to premature suture fusion, includes rare FGFR-related conditions such as Crouzon (CS), Muenke (MS), and Apert (AS) syndromes. These mutations affect skull but also brain development and are associated with variable neurodevelopmental outcomes. This brain impairment is still poorly described and understood, prompting for neuroimaging anatomical studies. We thus investigated regional brain growth and volumetric scaling in patients with these three syndromes and non-syndromic non-FGFR-related craniostenoses, using a normative modelling framework. We analyzed a rare set of brain MRI from 65 patients close to first cranial surgery time (30 CS among which 23 pre-surgery, 4 AS, 6 MS, 23 non-syndromic) and 130 typically developing controls. Millimetric 3D T1-weighted images were segmented into 6 cortical and 3 subcortical regions (AssemblyNet, Morphologist). After harmonization (ComBat), normative growth curves (Turner model) and static scaling curves (power-law model, effect of brain size regardless of age) were derived in controls. Patient deviations were assessed using permutation tests on mean normalized distance to typical model and abnormality rates (10th/90th percentiles). Patients with CS showed typical brain volumes for age except for enlarged ventricles, but slightly overscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Non-syndromic patients showed very similar volume distribution for age and brain size than CS ones. Patients with AS displayed increased total brain, temporal, cerebellar and central volumes for age, with overscaled temporal and cerebellar regions but underscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Patients with MS showed a similar, though milder, pattern: increased temporal volume for age, with temporal overscaling but frontal underscaling for frain size. Our findings reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR-related craniosynostoses, with a convergent pattern of temporal-frontal disproportions in AS and MS, associated with very specific mutations in the FGFR2 and 3 genes respectively, contrasting with a much more typical brain organization in more heterogeneous CS and non-syndromic patients. Beyond the pathophysiological meaning of these results, which call for a larger similar study covering as wide a range of patient variability as possible, our work highlights the relevance of normative modelling approach for characterizing rare craniofacial disorders using clinical MRI datasets.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Wavelet-derived indices of cardiac vagal and vasomotor oscillations as a new tool to better understand autonomic imbalance in post-COVID-19 dysautonomia

after.title: Preprint: Wavelet-derived indices of cardiac vagal and vasomotor oscillations as a new tool to better understand autonomic imbalance in post-COVID-19 dysautonomia
after.authors: Romero Fragoso, I.; Sainz-Jimenez, A.; Reyes Cruz, T.; Chiquete, E.; Tamez-Torres, K.; Sifuentes-Osornio, J.; Fossion, R.; Estanol, B.; Aceves-Buendia, J. d. J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Instituto Nacional de Ciencias Medicas y Nutricion Salvador Zubiran
after.abstract:
BackgroundWhen aiming to quantify autonomic imbalance, conventional heart rate variability (HRV) analysis generally reduces each posture to a single spectral value derived from interbeat intervals (IBI) alone. This analysis based only in IBI obscures transient events during blood pressure changes. We propose two wavelet-derived indices that quantify cardiac vagal and vasomotor sympathetic oscillations separately and over time. Since autonomic imbalance is directly related to baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), we evaluated them against an estimate of baroreflex sensitivity in post-COVID-19 patients.

MethodsIn this study, 121 participants (32 healthy controls and 89 patients with persistent post-COVID-19 autonomic symptoms) underwent an active standing test with continuous finger blood pressure. The continuous wavelet transform with generalized Morse wavelets yielded time-varying high-frequency power of IBI and low-frequency power of systolic blood pressure (SBP). Two new indices were proposed: Index I combined the magnitude and variability of HF IBI power (aimed to quantify parasympathetic activity), and the index J combined LF SBP power with the rate of its transient elevations (bursts), which aims to quantify sympathetic vasomotor activity; J/I was their ratio. Indices were computed for supine and orthostatic periods and compared with conventional HRV and BRS measurements.

ResultsIndex I correlated strongly with HF power of IBI and was lower in all patient subgroups than in controls, Index J had only a weak relation with LF power of IBI. On standing, J increased most in the subgroups with the worst baroreflex function. Orthostatic J/I was higher than in controls amongst patients, while LF/HF showed no differences. J/I was inversely correlated with BRS, most strongly when standing, and more strongly than LF/HF also. Adding J to I raised the cross-validated variance explained in orthostatic BRS substantially. In one example patient, a window during symptoms showed vasomotor oscillations that were hidden in the posture average.

ConclusionsWavelet-derived indices from routine beat-to-beat recordings separate cardiac vagal modulation from sympathetic vasomotor oscillations and their transients. J/I correlates with BRS impairment more closely than LF/HF, providing a potential alternative estimate of autonomic balance, and its time-resolved visual output allows analysis of clinically relevant windows within a posture. The new proposed variables allowed an evaluation of autonomic imbalance that could be applied to different pathologies.

items.title: Preprint: Integrated Genomic and Transcriptomic Profiling Reveals Distinct Biological Programs and Therapeutic Opportunities in Cancer of Unknown Primary

after.title: Preprint: Integrated Genomic and Transcriptomic Profiling Reveals Distinct Biological Programs and Therapeutic Opportunities in Cancer of Unknown Primary
after.authors: Wang, W.; Olsman, R.; Grashof, D. G. B.; Scheffers, L.; Leenders, M.; Robbrecht, D. G. J.; Snaebjornsson, P.; Katsikis, P. D.; van de Wouw, Y. A. J.; van de Werken, H. J. G.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Immunology, Erasmus MC, University Medical Center Rotterdam, Rotterdam, the Netherlands
after.abstract:
BackgroundCancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally. Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival. The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood. A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment.

MethodsWhole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations. Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes. Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA).

ResultsHigh-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins. Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes. The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2. GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes. Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation. These subtypes were not significantly associated with clinical or genomic features, indicating that the tumor microenvironment (TME) represents another layer of CUP heterogeneity. WGCNA further linked proliferative programs to cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and neuroendocrine features. WGS data identified potentially targetable alterations in 64% of the CUP patients.

ConclusionsCUP comprises biologically heterogeneous tumors with diverse predicted origins, mutational histories, and TME subtypes. Transcriptomic profiling and integrated genomics suggest that immune escape and rapid proliferation contribute to the clinical aggressive behavior. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for understanding CUP heterogeneity and support therapeutic stratification by both ToO predictions and tumor-specific molecular alterations.

after.title: Preprint: High-resolution spatiotemporal estimates of total and wildfire PM2.5 in the contiguous United States, 2018-2024: Implications for population exposure and mortality burden
after.authors: Liu, N.; Cheong, Y.; Larson, T.; Austin, E.; Seto, E.
after.abstract:
Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

after.authors: Liu, N.; Cheong, Y.; Larson, T.; Austin, E.; Seto, E.
after.abstract:
Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

data.label: Preprint: Comparing Misophonia with Clinical Emotional Dysregulation: A Multi-method Characterization Study
data.summary: added: Preprint: Comparing Misophonia with Clinical Emotional Dysregulation: A Multi-method Characterization Study

after.title: Preprint: Comparing Misophonia with Clinical Emotional Dysregulation: A Multi-method Characterization Study
after.authors: Brasher, Z. E.; Choi, J. Y.; Napolitano, S. C.; Neacsiu, A. D.
after.abstract: Background: Misophonia, a condition characterized by intense distress in response to specific everyday sounds, is increasingly recognized as distinct from established auditory and psychiatric disorders. Although it is associated with emotional dysregulation, impairment, distress, and atypical reactivity relative to clinical controls, few studies have directly compared misophonia with a diverse clinical sample exhibiting general difficulties managing emotions. This limits the understanding of its underlying mechanisms and hinders the development of targeted interventions. To address this gap, we conducted a multimethod study comparing adults with moderate-to-severe misophonia and adults with clinically significant emotion dysregulation. Methods: As part of a randomized controlled clinical trial, community-dwelling adults with elevated misophonia distress (n = 30) or clinically significant emotion dysregulation (n = 30) were enrolled in a study to examine sound responsiveness in misophonia. Participants completed a semi-structured clinical interview (SCID-5) and self-report measures assessing misophonia, emotional dysregulation, regulation, emotional processing, psychopathology, and contextual stress at intake. Next, physiological indices of arousal and regulation via skin conductance level (SCL), skin conductance response (SCR), and high-frequency heart rate variability (HF-HRV) were recorded during an Evocative Sound Challenge Task. Results: At baseline, participants with misophonia reported lower emotion dysregulation than the emotion dysregulation group, despite comparable self-report impairment attributable to emotional difficulties. Physiologically, participants with misophonia exhibited higher baseline HF-HRV than the emotion dysregulation group (p = .010). There was no evidence of a baseline difference in SCL (p = .157) or SCR (p = .085). During and after the sound task, groups differed in HF-HRV (ps = .002-.017), with the clinical group exhibiting higher HF-HRV than the misophonia group. No group differences were observed in SCL or SCR during and after the sound task after correcting for baseline (all ps > .08). Conclusion: Findings suggest that experiences of emotion dysregulation are relevant to misophonia but may differ from more generalized difficulties observed in clinically dysregulated populations. Despite endorsing substantial impairment, individuals with misophonia demonstrated lower global emotion dysregulation and greater emotion regulation self-efficacy, while physiological findings revealed distinct patterns of resting and task-related parasympathetic functioning. Collectively, the findings suggest that emotional difficulties in misophonia may be more context-dependent and closely tied to personally salient trigger cues than to generalized deficits in emotion regulation. Conceptualizing misophonia as pervasive emotion dysregulation may therefore conflate clinical impairment with the processes underlying symptom expression and obscure more targeted intervention mechanisms.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Timing the Target: Exploring the Circadian Transcriptome of Biologic Therapies in Asthma.

after.title: Preprint: Timing the Target: Exploring the Circadian Transcriptome of Biologic Therapies in Asthma.
after.authors: Akenroye, A.; Carey, V. J.; Scheer, F. A. J. L.; Weiss, S. T.
after.abstract: Background: Many of the immune pathways involved in asthma or in asthma treatment show circadian or diurnal variation. Understanding this variation can aid in biomarker discovery and/or therapy optimization. Objective: To evaluate if receptors, cytokines, and their pathways (n=46) targeted by currently approved biologics show significant diurnal rhythmicity and to identify their peak expression time. Methods: We used longitudinal bulk RNA sequencing datasets (discovery/replication cohorts: GSE113883 and GSE223613) and one microarray file (GSE39445) for cross-platform replication/validation. First, we used 16 canonical clock genes (including CLOCK, BMAL1, REV-ERB-beta) as positive controls to explore rhythmicity in each cohort. Thereafter, we evaluated if any targets of currently approved biologics or their corresponding receptors showed significant diurnal variation. For significant genes (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR<0.05), we estimated the baseline average, phase, peak-time of expression across the 24-hour day using clock time and quantified the cross-cohort consistency in the peak time of expression across the cohorts. Results: These cohorts included 453 longitudinal samples collected every two to four hours over a 24-28h cycle. Twelve (75%) of 16 evaluable clock genes showed significant rhythmicity. Only 34 of 46 (74%) asthma-related genes were evaluable across two or more cohorts. Of these 34 genes, 23 (68%) showed significant variation. Across all cohorts, the most preserved rhythmically expressed targets included many pathways or targets of monoclonal antibodies that are currently approved or in development: GATA3 and STAT6, master regulators of type 2 inflammation and IL4/IL13 signaling; chemokines, including the neutrophil chemoattractant, CXCL8; IL-5RA, benralizumab's target; FcRE1, suppressed by omalizumab; and IL1RL1(ST2) in clinical trials. Conclusion: Many therapeutic targets in asthma show significant diurnal rhythmicity. Future studies on how dosing time affects their therapeutic effectiveness while minimizing side effects are needed.

after.title: Preprint: Hybrid Video and Instance Segmentation for Surgical Scene Understanding in Robotic Mitral Valve Surgery
after.authors: Waldron, C.; Gulve, R. R.; Bhasin, N.; Al-Shoha, Z.; Eren, H.; Bhuiyan, N.; Zaky, M.; Ahmad, D.; Kandula, V.; Talapaneni, S.; Jernigan, E.; Pelletier, M.; Rahim, N.; Geirsson, A.; Mori, M.
after.abstract: Objective: Artificial intelligence-based surgical scene segmentation is fundamental to surgical scene understanding. However, the optimal segmentation strategy for robotic cardiac surgery remains unknown. We developed and evaluated a hybrid segmentation framework combining Mask R- CNN and Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) for surgical scene recognition during the entry phase of robotic mitral valve surgery. Methods: Intraoperative videos from ten robotic mitral valve operations performed at two institutions were analyzed. Seven anatomical structures and surgical object classes (ascending aorta, diaphragm, lung, pericardium, right atrium, robotic arms, and sutures) were manually annotated from 2172 image frames. We created three patient-level training, validation, and test splits after ruling out any split where an object class was completely missing from validation or test. Three segmentation approaches were compared: Mask R-CNN, Mask R-CNN-prompted SAM2 for all seven classes, and a hybrid late-fusion model combining SAM2 for anatomical structures and Mask R-CNN for robotic arms and sutures. Model performance was assessed using pixel accuracy, mean intersection over union (IoU), and Dice score. Results: Across the three patient-level splits, the hybrid late-fusion model achieved the highest average overall segmentation performance, with pixel accuracy of 0.79-0.91, mean IoU of 0.64-0.74, and mean Dice of 0.76-0.84. At the object level, late-fusion Dice scores across the three splits were 0.86-0.96 for aorta, 0.38-0.90 for diaphragm, 0.77-0.92 for lung, 0.48-0.77 for pericardium, 0.68- 0.90 for right atrium, 0.95-0.97 for robotic arms, and 0.66-0.76 for sutures. Mask R-CNN- prompted SAM2 outperformed Mask R-CNN for the aorta in all three splits and for the lung, pericardium, diaphragm, and right atrium in two of three splits, whereas Mask R-CNN was more reliable for sutures, including Dice scores of 0.76 vs 0.21 and 0.66 vs 0.53 in Splits 2 and 3. By combining prompted SAM2 for anatomy with Mask R-CNN for robotic arms and sutures, late fusion achieved the highest mean Dice in two of three splits (0.84 and 0.76) and the highest mean Dice averaged across all three splits; all-object SAM2 propagation performed slightly better in the remaining split (0.81 vs 0.80). Conclusions: A hybrid segmentation framework combining SAM2 and Mask R-CNN achieved the highest overall segmentation performance in two of three patient-level splits and performed comparably to the best-performing model in the remaining split. These findings suggest that object-specific hybrid segmentation strategies may improve surgical scene segmentation during robotic mitral valve surgery.

after.title: Preprint: High-resolution spatiotemporal estimates of total and wildfire PM2.5 in the contiguous United States, 2018-2024: Implications for population exposure and mortality burden
after.authors: Liu, N.; Cheong, Y.; Larson, T.; Austin, E.; Seto, E.
after.abstract:
Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

after.title: Preprint: Plasma Alzheimer''s assays agree on level but much less on individual rates of change
after.authors: Yang, Y.; Raymont, V.; Rowe, J. B.; Petersen, K. K.; Begde, A.; Brohier, R.; McEwen-Smith, R.; Koychev, I.; Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK
after.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Serial plasma testing is proposed for monitoring Alzheimer's disease and for trials, but its reliability for a person's rate of change is unknown. METHODS: In 393 ADNI participants with three plasma samples over a median 5.0 years, 15 measures of five biomarkers were assayed on aliquots of the same samples, separating shared change from assay-specific variation at each sampling occasion. Results were tested in 1,093 A4/LEARN participants. RESULTS: Assays agreed well on cross-sectional levels (intraclass correlation 0.75--0.95 for pTau217, pTau181, GFAP, NfL) but less on individual rates of change (0.44, 95% CI 0.37--0.50, for pTau217). Assay-specific slope variance was approximately zero, so disagreement was predominantly random. Three-sample single-assay slope reliability was at most 0.40 (0.34--0.46) for pTau217, 0.42 (0.33--0.51) for pTau181, 0.47 (0.37--0.60) for GFAP, 0.52 (0.40--0.64) for NfL, and 0.10 (0.03--0.20) for A{beta}42/40. Two pTau217 measurements had to differ by 65%--131%, depending on the assay, to exceed measurement noise. Detecting 25% slowing of pTau217 change required 924 (598--1,468) to 4,030 (2,091--9,256) participants per arm, or 532 (357--778) to 965 (655--1,431) with averaged measures. In A4/LEARN, single-assay pTau217 reliability was 0.54 (0.46--0.61), and a 7.3- rather than 4.8-year span raised it by 0.10 (0.00-0.22); a fourth sample within it added little. DISCUSSION: With three single-assay samples, much of an individual's measured change is noise. Longer spans, endpoint replication, and assay choice, rather than additional intermediate samples, are needed for reliable serial testing and trials.

after.authors: Michel, N.; Tran, K. T.; Reddy, N.; Scott, J. C.; Gur, R. C.; Visoki, E.; Bren, Z.; Moore, T. M.; Barzilay, R.
after.abstract: Background: Cannabis use has rapidly emerged as a significant factor associated with risk of suicidal ideation or attempts (suicidality) in adolescents and young adults. Although the mechanism underlying this association remains uncertain, cognition is a candidate explanatory pathway. Method: We analyzed longitudinal data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (N = 10,228; mean age at end of 4-year follow-up 14.17 years, 52.5% male, and 47.5% female). We included three cannabis exposure definitions: one-time experimentation, initiation (more than one-time cannabis use), or ever use. Outcomes included suicidal ideation (SI) and suicide attempt (SA). Mixed-effects regression models quantified associations between cannabis exposures and outcomes adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, household income, and parental education. Additional analyses examined associations of cannabis use with four NIH Toolbox cognitive measures previously linked to suicidality (flanker, working memory, picture vocabulary, and picture sequence memory), and associations of these cognitive measures with SI and SA. Results: Cannabis use was associated with increased odds of SI (ever use odds ratio (OR)=3.18, 95% confidence interval (95%CI) =2.52-4.00) and SA (OR=4.86, 95%CI=3.36-7.03), associations were overall similar across all exposure definitions (all p < 0.001). Cannabis use was also associated with lower performance across multiple cognitive domains ({beta} = -0.08 to -0.16, all p < 0.05). Better cognitive performance, specifically in episodic memory, was associated with lower suicidality: SI (OR = 0.91, 95%CI=0.86-0.95) and SA (OR = 0.88, 95%CI=0.80- 0.97). Conclusion: These findings support cognition as a potential mechanism linking cannabis use to adolescent suicide risk and warrant longitudinal investigation.

after.authors: Ly, C.; Liu, C.; Ciarcia, J.; Lee, S.; Johnston, K. J. A.; Kepinska, A. P.; Huckins, L. M.
after.abstract: Psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) are common during adolescence (prevalence: 17-60%), however, sex differences in the biopsychosocial factors associated with PLEs, particularly pubertal development and sex hormones, and PLE trajectories remains less understood. Here, we leverage data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study to examine genetic, psychosocial, and hormonal correlates of PLE risk and persistence in 7,870 adolescents reporting at least one PLE across BL to Y3 follow-up. Among individuals of European ancestry, higher genetic risk for schizophrenia was positively associated with PLEs. Sex stratified multivariate linear regression analyses revealed sex-specific differences in associations between social factors and the outcome, with parent acceptance (beta= -0.09, p = 2.47x10-02 in males; beta = -0.44, p = 1.5x10-20 in females) and overt aggression (beta = 0.038, p = 1.67x10-02 in males; beta = -0.081, p = 1.53x10-05 in females) showing differing directions and magnitudes of effect in males and females. Pubertal development in males and females and age of menarche are associated with PLE risk, while mediation analyses identified estradiol in females as a mediator of the association between puberty and PLEs in premenarchal females. Lastly, multivariate logistic regression analyses and Analysis of Variance showed that higher exposure to psychosocial risk factors, such as discrimination (OR = 1.47, p = 1.11x10-04) and social victimization (OR = 1.05, p = 2.02x10-02), earlier pubertal development, and earlier age of menarche predict membership to the persistent PLE trajectory. These findings highlight sex-specific social correlates of adolescent PLEs and implicate pubertal timing and hormonal pathways in PLE risk and persistence. Understanding how genetic, social, and biological factors jointly shape PLE trajectories may help inform early identification of psychosis risk.

after.authors: Mushobekwa Biringanine, W.; Rugajo, N.; Ntibonera Aganze, J.; Cito Mudekereza, O.; Kabagale Ansima, C.; Zigashane Kawala, L.; Lurhangire Ongezi, E.; lupande Mwenebitu, D.
after.abstract: Abstract Background: Community pharmacies are often the first point of care in low and middleincome countries, yet the knowledge, attitudes and practices (KAP) of their workers regarding antibiotics and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) are undocumented in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Objectives: To assess KAP regarding antibiotic use and AMR, and their determinants, among community pharmacy workers in Bukavu, Eastern DRC. Methods: A cross sectional survey was conducted in April to June 2026 among 423 community pharmacy workers, one per pharmacy, selected by multistage sampling across the three health zones of Bukavu, using a structured, interviewer administered questionnaire. Knowledge (8 items), attitudes (9 items) and dispensing practices (4 items) were scored using modified Bloom s cut offs. Multivariable logistic regression identified determinants. Results: Good knowledge was found in 19.4%, favourable attitudes in 17.5% and appropriate dispensing practices in 27.4%. Overall, 96.5% dispensed antibiotics without a prescription and 9.2% knew the WHO AWaRe classification. University education and pharmaceutical qualification were independently associated with good knowledge [adjusted OR (aOR) 4.38 and 2.41] and appropriate practices (aOR 5.74 and 2.01). Good knowledge was associated with favourable attitudes (aOR 4.86, 95% CI 2.68 to 8.82), which in turn predicted appropriate practices (aOR 6.62, 95% CI 3.50 to 12.53). In addition, 57.0% knew of Machange, an informal mixture of medicines: 99.6% of those describing its composition listed at least one antibiotic, and 65.6% of those familiar with it sold it. Conclusions: Community pharmacy workers in Bukavu show substantial gaps in antibioticrelated KAP. Stewardship interventions should combine education with regulation, diagnostic capacity and AMR surveillance within a One Health framework. Keywords: antimicrobial resistance; One Health; community pharmacists; antibiotic misuse; antimicrobial stewardship; knowledge, attitudes and practices; Democratic Republic of Congo

after.abstract: Background: Evidence linking social, behavioral, and environmental factors to dementia in Central Africa remains limited. Objective: To examine associations between 16 factors and dementia status in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and quantify incremental model fit beyond age and sex. Methods: This cross sectional analysis included 721 participants (232 cognitively unimpaired; 489 with dementia, including 247 with suspected Alzheimers disease). Logistic regression jointly modeled 16 factors, age, sex, and missing-category indicators. Continuous covariates with missing values were mean-imputed and standardized. Model fit was assessed using Nagelkerke pseudo R squared, likelihood-ratio testing, and 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Results: Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 increased from 0.106 with age and sex to 0.368 after adding the factors (change in R2 = 0.262; bootstrap 95% CI: 0.241-0.371; chi-square(27) = 163.62, p < 0.001). Poverty (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.52-3.60), low resilience (aOR = 1.84, 95% CI: 1.18-2.86), and depression (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.02-2.31) were associated with higher dementia odds. Higher education (aOR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.39-0.66, per standard deviation increase) and obesity (aOR = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.10-0.90) showed inverse associations; obesity data were 79.9% missing. Alcohol consumption and PM2.5 exposure were not significantly associated with dementia. Conclusions: Poverty, lower resilience, depression, and education were associated with dementia status in this nonrepresentative cohort. Incremental model fit does not quantify preventable dementia burden, and causality cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional data.

Methods: This cross sectional analysis included 721 participants (232 cognitively unimpaired; 489 with dementia, including 247 with suspected Alzheimers disease). Logistic regression jointly modeled 16 factors, age, sex, and missing-category indicators. Continuous covariates with missing values were mean-imputed and standardized. Model fit was assessed using Nagelkerke pseudo R squared, likelihood-ratio testing, and 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Results: Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 increased from 0.106 with age and sex to 0.368 after adding the factors (change in R2 = 0.262; bootstrap 95% CI: 0.241-0.371; chi-square(27) = 163.62, p < 0.001). Poverty (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.52-3.60), low resilience (aOR = 1.84, 95% CI: 1.18-2.86), and depression (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.02-2.31) were associated with higher dementia odds. Higher education (aOR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.39-0.66, per standard deviation increase) and obesity (aOR = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.10-0.90) showed inverse associations; obesity data were 79.9% missing. Alcohol consumption and PM2.5 exposure were not significantly associated with dementia. Conclusions: Poverty, lower resilience, depression, and education were associated with dementia status in this nonrepresentative cohort. Incremental model fit does not quantify preventable dementia burden, and causality cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional data.

after.abstract: Abstract Background: -Synuclein seed amplification assay (Syn-SAA) has emerged as a promising biomarker for detecting underlying -synuclein pathology and predicting phenoconversion in prodromal Parkinson's disease (PD). However, its association with longitudinal clinical progression during the prodromal stage remains unclear. We investigated whether baseline Syn-SAA status and kinetic parameters were associated with motor and cognitive progression and subsequent phenoconversion in prodromal individuals. Methods: Clinical progression was assessed using the Movement Disorder Society-Sponsored Revision of the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III motor scores, Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) stage, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores. Linear mixed-effects models were utilized to examine the associations between baseline Syn-SAA status, kinetic parameters, and longitudinal changes in these clinical measures. Additionally, time-to-event analyses were performed to assess the associations between SAA measurements and phenoconversion to PD or dementia with Lewy bodies. Results: We identified 2,532 participants with available baseline Syn-SAA status in the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) prodromal cohort. This longitudinal study, which included up to 12 years of follow-up, comprised 1,714 Syn-SAA-positive and 818 Syn-SAA-negative individuals. Over the follow-up period, Syn-SAA-positive participants exhibited significantly faster motor progression measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III motor score than Syn-SAA-negative participants (0.611 vs. 0.139 points/year; P<0.001). This association persisted after excluding phenoconverters (0.430 vs. 0.202 points/year; P=0.014) and restricting follow-up to seven years (0.588 vs. 0.137 points/year; P<0.001). Among the 1,796 participants included in the time-to-event analyses, 181 phenoconversion events occurred. Baseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with a significantly higher hazard of phenoconversion (adjusted hazard ratio 5.72, 95% confidence interval 3.78-8.68; P<0.001), whereas kinetic parameters showed no significant associations with phenoconversion risk. Conclusions: Baseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with accelerated motor progression during the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion. These findings support the potential utility of Syn-SAA positivity as a prognostic biomarker for motor progression and phenoconversion, with implications for risk stratification and participant selection in future disease-modifying trials.

after.title: Preprint: Limited English Proficiency and Rates of Dilated Eye Examinations Among U.S. Adults with Diabetes
after.authors: Lam, S. Z.; Xing, E.; Sun, G.
after.abstract: Purpose: To determine whether English proficiency is associated with diabetic retinopathy screening rates among patients with diabetes in the United States. Design: A retrospective, cross-sectional study. Participants: Individuals with diabetes who responded to the Medicare Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), a nationally representative survey of U.S. households (2013-2022). Methods: Survey-weighted, multivariable logistic regression. Main Outcome Measures: Adjusted odds ratio (aOR) of 1) having ever received a dilated fundus examination (DFE) and 2) having received consecutive year DFEs. Results: The analytic sample included 11,441 respondents representing a weighted sample of 15,107,166 U.S. civilians with diabetes per year from 2013-2022. The mean age was 62 years (SD: 14 years), and 50% were female. Individuals with limited English proficiency (LEP) comprised 11.6% of the cohort. Respondents with LEP had lower odds of ever having received a DFE compared to English-proficient respondents (aOR=0.729, 95% CI: 0.541-0.976). The association between having consecutive year DFEs and English proficiency was non-significant (aOR=1.189, 95% CI: 0.917-1.541). In sensitivity analyses using a definition of LEP as speaking English less than well, LEP was associated with lower odds of ever having a DFE (aOR=0.632, 95% CI: 0.460-0.869) and higher odds of consecutive year exams (aOR=1.415, 95% CI: 1.057-1.896). Conclusions: LEP status was associated with lower odds of ever having had a DFE and equal or greater odds of having consecutive year DFEs. Efforts to reduce language-related disparities for patients with LEP should focus on improving initial access to ophthalmologic care.

after.title: Preprint: Maternal vitamin D status during pregnancy is associated with reduced DNA methylation entropy and hypomethylation of regulatory regions related to immune tolerance
after.authors: Boyd, S.; Hecker, J.; Mirzakhani, H.; DeMeo, D. L.; Weiss, S. T.; Halu, A.
after.abstract: Background Vitamin D is crucial to maternal immune system function during pregnancy, acting via the vitamin D receptor (VDR). Yet, there is widespread vitamin D insufficiency among pregnant women. The Vitamin D Antenatal Asthma Reduction Trial investigated the effect of maternal vitamin D on offspring asthma/wheeze. Pregnant women were randomized to a vitamin D supplementation or placebo group, and maternal blood samples were collected at 10-18 and 32-38 weeks of gestation. This analysis aims to identify associations between 25-hydroxyvitamin-D3 (25OHD) and DNA methylation (DNAm). DNAm data were obtained with Illumina Infinium Methylation EPICv2 array. Linear mixed effects models assessed DNAm-25OHD associations, adjusting for demographic and clinical factors. Probe-level results were aggregated to identify differentially methylated regions (DMRs), which were annotated to genes via proximity to promoters or enhancers. In addition, DNAm entropy was investigated for associations with 25OHD. Results Hypomethylated (meso-/hyper-methylated) DMRs showed negative (positive) DNAm-25OHD associations. DMRs overlapped with vitamin D-sensitive topologically associating domains and open chromatin. Annotated genes were primarily enriched for pathways related to antigen processing/presentation. Using paired RNA-seq data, the expression of 59 annotated genes was significantly associated with DNAm of its corresponding DMR. These included IKBKB, a kinase with suppressive effects on the NF-kappa-B pathway. Furthermore, DMRs showed negative entropy-25OHD associations, suggesting a more homogeneous immune methylome in women with higher 25OHD levels. Conclusions Our findings suggest that increased vitamin D may promote methylome stability in genomic regions associated with antigen presentation and immune tolerance, conveying a complex regulatory landscape of the vitamin D-associated methylome during pregnancy.

after.abstract: Gene-by-environment (GxE) interactions inform where genetics and environment converge to impact human health and disease. However, systematically mapping GxE interactions has been challenging due to the diversity of testable exposures and a lack of scalable approaches to measure the environments cells experience in vivo. Here, we identified modules of correlated plasma metabolites and proteins and used them as quantitative proxies for environmental exposures experienced by circulating leukocytes. We demonstrated that these proxies are associated with environmentally modifiable clinical traits such as diet and infection and support broad mapping of geneby environment (GxE) interactions affecting gene expression and CpG methylation in leukocytes. We identified significant interactions for 95.2% of tested genes and 5.9% of tested methylation sites. These GxE interactions showed specificity to exposures and cell type. Colocalization analysis further provided links between interactions and complex trait and disease loci. Finally, we expanded GxE interaction mapping to unexplored cell types using a zero-shot transfer model to predict GxE interactions in held-out cell types, demonstrating how plasma metabolomics and proteomics can enhance the discovery of GxE interactions across the body. Altogether, this work provides a systematic multi-omic framework to study how gene regulation is shaped by both the genome and the molecular environments cells experience in vivo.

after.abstract: To leverage independent genetic evidence from multiple species, we developed a cross-species gene-based GWAS meta-analysis framework and applied this to Dizygotic Twinning (DZT) in humans and cattle. After meta-analysis within species, we converted human and cattle GWAS summary statistics to gene-level association signals within each species, mapped genes across species through human-cattle orthology, and then combined gene-level evidence for orthologous genes across the two species. DZT is defined as giving birth to multiple offspring after a single pregnancy resulting from spontaneous multiple ovulation. In humans, DZT occurs in about 1% of pregnancies with heritability estimates of 20% to 30% whilst in cattle DZT occurs in 1-5% of pregnancies and heritability is estimated at about 11%. Here, we present the largest human GWAS meta-analysis including data from 1,395,285 participants. We identified 16 genetic regions of interest, including 12 independent loci from the SNP based analyses and 4 genes identified in the gene-based MAGMA analyses. Among the prioritized genes are follicle stimulation hormone receptor (FSHR) and growth differentiation factor 9 (GDF9), that both are involved in ovarian folliculogenesis. Cattle GWAS summary statistics were based on data from 2,656 Irish Holstein bulls with estimated breeding values for predisposition to twinning based on 2,238,936 birth records, and 86,391 German Holstein dams. After combining the gene-level analyses for 13,225 genes mapped as orthologous across the human and cattle data we identify FSHR as a central locus for DZT in both humans and cattle. We find evidence of additional associations, including ACVR2A, which plays a role in embryonic implantation and TUFM, which has previously been implicated in premature ovarian insufficiency. Our approach provides a promising framework for future cross-species comparative GWAS studies. It shows benefits for gene discovery and gene prioritization and in our application expands available functional follow-up data, allowing us to leverage cattle eQTL data to resolve human GWAS loci. The method and underlying philosophy presented here are transferable to other shared phenotypes across several species.

after.authors: Shisanya, M. S.; Namusonge, L. N.; Simiyu, C. M.; Kirwa, T. C.; Morema, E. N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Kibabii University, School of Nursing, Department of Community Health and Mental Health Nursing, Bungoma, Kenya
after.abstract: Objectives: To assess the completeness, consistency, plausibility, uniqueness and analytical usability of routine maternity and newborn records used for preterm and small newborn care, and how facility health-information-system readiness and working conditions explain these patterns. Design: Multicentre cross-sectional mixed-methods study of routine health data with embedded explanatory qualitative interviews. Setting: Twelve health facilities (levels 3-5) in Bungoma and one neighbouring county, Western Kenya. Participants: 349 maternity-register and 291 newborn records for deliveries from July 2024 to May 2026; 10 facility readiness assessments; two provider key informant interviews. Primary and secondary outcome measures: Variable- and record-level completeness from original uncleaned abstractions; prespecified consistency and plausibility rule violations; duplicates; agreement between recorded and rule-derived preterm, low-birth-weight (LBW) and very-low-birth-weight classifications. Results: Median record completeness was 100% (IQR 94.7-100) for register and 93.5% (IQR 84.8-100) for newborn records; a complete core record was present in 175/349 (50.1%, 95% CI 44.9 to 55.4) and 77/291 (26.5%, 95% CI 21.7 to 31.8) respectively. No maternal age, gestational age, birth weight or Apgar value was implausible, but chronological errors were common: recorded and date-derived length of stay differed by >1 day in 92/225 (40.9%) and admission preceded birth in 35/257 (13.6%). Agreement with rule-derived classification was high for very low birth weight (kappa 0.89, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.95) but moderate for LBW (kappa 0.53, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.73; McNemar p=0.001). Complete documentation was more likely with three or more record sources (adjusted prevalence ratio 1.80, 95% CI 1.05 to 3.08) and less likely for newborns who died (0.46, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.84). Providers described documentation competing with workload. Conclusions: Identification, gestational age, birth weight and disposition were documented sufficiently for classification and mortality analysis; timing fields, maternal history and transport variables were not. Preterm-birth prevalence was not estimable without an all-delivery denominator.

after.abstract: Diagnosis and risk stratification of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) rely on the detection of diverse genetic aberrations using multiple standard-of-care (SoC) assays. With the increasing number of clinically relevant alterations and limited resolution of SoC methods, whole-genome and transcriptome sequencing (WGTS) represents a promising alternative. In this multi-center study, we evaluated the technical feasibility and clinical performance of WGTS across five sites in Sweden by comparison with SoC diagnostics. A total of 235 patients (197 adults and 38 children) underwent parallel SoC testing and WGTS analysis. WGTS identified 57/58 (98%) clinically relevant gene rearrangements detected by SoC and revealed an additional 12 rearrangements, including RUNX1::RUNX1T1, KMT2A and NUP98 rearrangements. For structural variants and copy-number variants, WGS showed 90% concordance with SoC, with discrepancies mainly involving subclonal events or tetraploidy. For gene mutations, WGS achieved 94% sensitivity, detecting all NPM1, CEBPA bZIP, and IDH1/2 mutations, but missing low-frequency FLT3-ITDs. Tumor-only analysis performed comparably to paired analysis for clinically relevant variants. Diagnostic classification was highly concordant between WGTS and SoC (WHO: 94%; ICC: 93%), with improved genetic subclassification in 5 - 6% of cases by WGTS. ELN risk stratification was concordant in 97% with WGTS reclassifying 2% of patients. Finally, a ring trial involving seven cases demonstrated complete agreement across sites in identifying aberrations. In conclusion, WGTS is a feasible and accurate comprehensive diagnostic approach for AML in a decentralized setting, improving detection of clinically relevant aberrations. However, complementary high-sensitivity assays for FLT3-ITD remain necessary for routine clinical implementation.

after.abstract: Background: Urticaria (hives) is a common inflammatory skin disorder affecting approximately 20% of the population during their lifetime. Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) and delayed pressure urticaria (DPU) can substantially impair quality of life, and treatment remains challenging, particularly in refractory DPU. Although neutrophils are well-recognized components of urticarial skin infiltrates, their functional contribution and therapeutic relevance remain poorly understood. Objective: To characterize neutrophil-associated inflammation in CSU and DPU, assess its relationship to disease control, and explore potential therapeutic targets. Methods: Skin biopsies from patients with CSU (n = 4-17) and DPU (n = 5-15) and healthy controls (HC; n = 5) were examined by immunofluorescence for neutrophil infiltration, NET formation, and IL-17A and IL-23 positivity. Peripheral neutrophils were characterized by flow cytometry (CSU n = 8, DPU n = 5, HC n = 5) and circulating MPO-DNA complexes were measured by ELISA (CSU n = 33, DPU n = 29). Patients with refractory DPU received tildrakizumab on an individual off-label basis (n = 8). Disease activity, disease control and quality of life were assessed using the weekly Urticaria Activity Score (UAS7), the Urticaria Control Test (UCT) and the Chronic Urticaria Quality of Life Questionnaire (CU-Q2oL). Neutrophil activation markers were compared between patients receiving tildrakizumab (n = 8) and those without tildrakizumab treatment (n = 11). Paired measurements before and during treatment were evaluated in three patients. Results: Despite similar overall dermal neutrophil infiltration, DPU showed greater neutrophil accumulation in the deep dermis than CSU. This spatial difference was accompanied by more pronounced NET formation in DPU. Higher NET-associated tissue signals correlated with poorer disease control in DPU, whereas no significant correlation was observed in CSU. Evidence of enhanced neutrophil activation in DPU also extended to the circulation, with increased CD66b and decreased CD62L expression compared with both CSU and HC. Circulating MPO-DNA levels were elevated in DPU relative to the HC reference, although the direct comparison between DPU and CSU was not significant. Investigation of the IL-23/IL-17 axis revealed IL-17A-positive neutrophils and IL-23-positive cells in lesional skin of both subtypes, with no significant difference in the proportion of IL-17A-positive neutrophils or IL-23-positive cells between CSU and DPU. In an exploratory therapeutic assessment, tildrakizumab treatment was associated with an overall significantly improved disease activity, control and quality of life in patients from week 0 to week 12. CD11b and CD66b expression was lower in treated than untreated patients, while paired analyses showed heterogeneous changes in neutrophil activation markers. Conclusion: The combined tissue and blood findings suggest a more prominent role for neutrophil-associated inflammatory processes in DPU than in CSU. The presence of IL-17A-positive neutrophils and IL-23-positive cells in lesional skin provides a rationale for investigating the contribution of this cytokine pathway. Exploratory observations under tildrakizumab support further evaluation of IL-23 inhibition in refractory DPU, while its effects on neutrophil-associated inflammation require confirmation.

after.abstract: Background: Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer in men and women, and the fifth most common cancer overall, in South Africa. A previous report by the South African National Cancer Registry (SANCR) established that colorectal cancer incidence is rising in all South African population groups but rising fastest in Black South Africans. However, whether incidence increases by age at onset, as observed in many upper-income countries worldwide, remains unknown. In the present study, we assessed changes in colorectal cancer incidence (2002-2023) and mortality (2002-2019) in South Africa by sex, population group and age at onset. Methods: We calculated incidence from SANCR case counts and mortality from Stats SA death records, using Stats SA mid-year population estimates, standardised to the Segi world standard population. We defined age at onset as early (less than 50 years) or late (50 years or older). We described trends using joinpoint regression and annual percentage changes (APCs) over 2002-2023 and 2011-2023, the period after private-laboratory reporting became mandatory. Results: A total of 70,467 histologically confirmed primary colorectal cancers were registered with the SANCR over 2002-2023; 53.7% were in men. The overall age-standardised incidence rate (ASIR) was 6.61 per 100,000 (95% CI 6.32-6.89) in 2002 and 8.23 (7.99-8.46) in 2023. Overall incidence fell from 2002 to 2007 (not significant), rose from 2007 to 2015 and showed no significant change from 2015 to 2023. The first two segments coincide with the withdrawal of some private laboratories from reporting in 2005-2007 and with mandatory reporting from 2011. From 2011 to 2023, incidence fell in White South Africans (APC -1.0%, 95% CI -1.9 to -0.04), rose in Black African South Africans (+3.1%, 2.0 to 4.2) and did not change significantly in Coloured (-1.0%, -2.3 to 0.3) or Indian/Asian (+0.3%, -2.2 to 2.7) South Africans. Early-onset incidence rose by 1.6% per year (95% CI 1.1 to 2.1) over 2002-2023, similar to late-onset incidence (1.8%, 1.0 to 2.5). After 2011, neither changed significantly (early-onset +0.3%, -0.3 to 0.9; late-onset 0.0%, -1.0 to 1.0). Over 2002-2023, the early-onset APC was highest in White South Africans (+3.9%, 2.9 to 4.9), followed by Black African (+1.7%, 1.1 to 2.4), Coloured (+1.6%, 1.0 to 2.3) and Indian/Asian (+1.5%, 0.4 to 2.7) South Africans. The late-onset APC was +4.1% (3.4 to 4.9) in Black African, +1.3% (0.1 to 2.5) in White, +1.3% (0.1 to 2.5) in Indian/Asian and +0.7% (-0.3 to 1.6) in Coloured South Africans. After 2011, early-onset incidence rose in White (+1.2%, 0.3 to 2.2), Coloured (+1.7%, 0.4 to 3.1) and Black African (+1.1%, 0.4 to 1.8) South Africans. Late-onset incidence fell in White South Africans (-1.5%, -2.6 to -0.4) and rose in Black African South Africans (+3.7%, 2.4 to 5.0). Early-onset mortality rose by 1.2% per year (0.5 to 2.0) over 2002-2019, and late-onset mortality by 0.9% (0.3 to 1.4). Conclusion: Early-onset colorectal cancer incidence in South Africa rose over 2002-2023, and much of the rise coincided with mandatory private-laboratory reporting from 2011. Since 2011, early-onset incidence has risen modestly in White, Coloured and Black African South Africans, while late-onset incidence has fallen in White South Africans. In Black African South Africans, late-onset incidence and mortality continue to rise faster than early-onset.

after.abstract: Background Comprehensive influenza surveillance is conducted year-round in the United States to monitor changes in influenza activity. This report summarizes the 2025-26 U.S. influenza season. Methods Data from September 28, 2025 through October 3, 2026 were collected from national surveillance systems monitoring influenza through laboratory testing, outpatient and emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and mortality. Data modeled disease burden and assessed severity using established criteria. A subset of influenza positive specimens were genetically and antigenically characterized and assessed for antiviral susceptibility. Results Influenza activity peaked during the week ending December 27, 2025, five weeks earlier than the 2024-25 season. There were two waves of influenza activity with influenza A(H3N2) subclade K viruses predominating the season overall and during the first wave followed by a smaller B/Victoria wave. The majority of circulating A(H3N2) and B/Victoria viruses were antigenically drifted from 2025-26 influenza vaccine reference strains. Season severity was classified as moderate overall, with children (0-17 years old) experiencing a high severity season and adults experiencing a moderate severity season. Children experienced the highest percent of influenza-associated outpatient and emergency department visits compared to other age groups. This season's cumulative influenza-associated hospitalization rate in children is the highest hospitalization rate in the past 16 years. Additionally, there were 198 influenza-associated pediatric deaths reported to CDC as of October 29, 2026. Conclusions Although antigenically drifted A(H3N2) viruses predominated, the 2025-26 U.S. influenza season occurred within historic norms for timing and severity. Year-round surveillance remains critical for detecting changes in influenza viruses and monitoring influenza-associated morbidity and mortality.

after.title: Preprint: High-resolution spatiotemporal estimates of total and wildfire PM2.5 in the contiguous United States, 2018-2024: Implications for population exposure and mortality burden
after.authors: Liu, N.; Cheong, Y.; Larson, T.; Austin, E.; Seto, E.
after.abstract:
Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

after.title: Preprint: Prospective multi-omic profiling identifies predictive and genetically supported molecular determinants of incident epilepsy
after.authors: Hassanin, E.; Omidvar, M. E.; Panda, P.; Lerche, H.; Leu, C.; Lal, D.; May, P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, University of Luxembourg, Esch-Sur-Alzette, Luxembourg
after.abstract: Abstract Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, yet biomarkers capable of identifying individuals at risk before clinical onset are lacking, and the molecular mechanisms preceding disease onset remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated plasma proteomic, metabolomic, and genomic data from the UK Biobank to characterize molecular changes preceding epilepsy and evaluate their predictive and causal relevance. We quantified 2,923 plasma proteins in 53,000 participants and followed incident epilepsy for up to 15 years before epilepsy diagnosis. Cox proportional hazards analyses identified 116 proteins associated with incident epilepsy, led by neurofilament light chain (NEFL; HR=2.03) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15; HR=1.73). These proteins were enriched for extracellular signaling, immune regulation, and cell-death pathways and displayed distinct subtype- and age-specific signatures. A proteomic risk score comprising 32 proteins stratified epilepsy risk, with individuals in the highest quintile exhibiting a 3.5-fold greater risk than those in the lowest quintile (AUC=0.70). In parallel, 154 of 249 circulating metabolites were associated with incident epilepsy, with the strongest inverse association observed for citrate (HR=0.72) and positive associations across HDL-related metabolites (HR=1.16-1.21), implicating dysregulated energy and lipoprotein metabolism. A metabolomic risk score showed more modest discrimination (AUC=0.63). Integrating proteomic, metabolomic, polygenic, and demographic information yielded an overall AUC of 0.71 for incident epilepsy; in a separate cross-sectional analysis of individuals with early-onset epilepsy discrimination reached an AUC of 0.79. Proteome-wide cis-pQTL Mendelian randomization identified 12 proteins associated with epilepsy after false discovery rate correction, predominantly for genetic generalized epilepsy. O-GlcNAcase (OGA), a regulator of protein O-GlcNAcylation with established roles in neuronal function and synaptic plasticity, showed the strongest protective association (OR=0.71, FDR=2.7 e-8). Serine protease 53 (PRSS53), a poorly characterized serine protease, showed strong evidence for a potential shared causal variant with epilepsy (colocalization PP.H4=0.95). Together, these findings demonstrate that circulating molecular alterations precede epilepsy diagnosis by years and reveal complementary proteomic, metabolic, and genetic determinants of disease susceptibility, providing a framework for biologically informed risk stratification and therapeutic target prioritization.

after.authors: Takashima, M.; Ullman, A. J.; Day, T.; Ware, R. S.
after.abstract: Background: Up to 20% of hospitalised infants with a peripheral intravenous catheter (PIVC) have an infusate-related injury. The PATCH trial is testing whether an IV biosensor (ivWatch) added to standard observation reduces infiltration and extravasation injuries compared with standard observation alone. Methods: PATCH is a multicentre, type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation randomised controlled trial at three Queensland hospitals. Infants under 1 year (weighing at least 1000 g) with a PIVC expected to remain more than 24 hours for intermediate- or high-risk infusates, antimicrobials or continuous fluids are randomised 1:1, stratified by site (four strata). The target sample is 532. Analysis: The primary outcome is any infiltration/extravasation injury (mild to severe harm, CCHMC Extravasation Harm Scale), confirmed by a blinded outcome assessment committee. The primary analysis follows intention to treat and uses logistic regression adjusted for randomisation stratum. The risk difference is estimated by standardisation, with the odds ratio also reported. Secondary outcomes include injury severity, time to PIVC failure, dwell time, replacement PIVC, skin injuries and serious adverse events. This plan was finalised on 10/11/2026, during recruitment and before database lock or any unblinded analysis. Trial registration: ACTRN12623000561684.

after.title: Preprint: Active Health Problems in Real-World Consultations on a Purpose-Built Medical AI Platform
after.authors: Adamson, B.; Li, A. W.; Gilson, S.; Waxse, B.; Ambwani, G.; Crowe, B.; Oskowitz, A.
after.abstract: Importance: Consumers use conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for health at scale, but whether purpose-built medical AI is used primarily for information seeking or as an entry point into care remains unclear. Objective: To characterize the clinical concepts users present, their visit intentions, and progression to physician telehealth care in real-world consultations on a purpose-built medical AI platform. Design: Exploratory retrospective cohort study of consultations sampled in equal monthly numbers between June 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026. Setting: A free, publicly available, consumer-facing, anonymous-by-default medical AI platform. Participants: Random sample of 26,000 English-language consultations by users aged 18 years or older, each with at least 5 chat interaction rounds. Exposure: A chat consultation with the medical AI. Main Outcomes and Measures: Clinical concepts linked approximately to SNOMED CT; visit intentions classified with a prespecified 11-category schema and reclassified with a published 12-category consumer-health taxonomy; completion of the AI consult with a structured SOAP note; and progression to a completed physician telehealth visit. Automated extraction pipelines were validated against physician annotation in a random subsample. Results: Of 26,000 sampled consultations, 56.7% were by users recorded as female and 50.9% by users aged 18 to 34 years. Among 25,975 consultations with successful extraction, 77,597 clinical concepts were identified; headache, abdominal pain, fatigue, and fever were the most common presenting concepts. Of 55,257 classified intentions, 60.1% (95% CI, 59.7%-60.5%) concerned a new or worsening condition. When consultations were reclassified with the published consumer-health taxonomy, 74.3% (95% CI, 73.8%-74.8%) included symptom questions or health concerns, whereas 5.0% (95% CI, 4.7%-5.2%) included health information or education, reversing the rank order published for a general-purpose assistant. Overall, 53.9% of sampled consultations ended with a structured SOAP note, and 15.1% of those progressed to a completed physician telehealth review. Conclusions and Relevance: Users of this purpose-built medical AI platform predominantly presented active personal health problems rather than general information requests. Symptom-driven use, generation of structured clinical documentation, and progression to physician care suggest that purpose-built medical AI may function as an entry point to clinical care for some users.

after.title: Preprint: Manifestation-Guided Adaptation of CT Foundation Model for Early Neurological Prognosis after ECPR
after.authors: Kaviany, A.; Mutirangura, P.; Goyal, S.; Bentho, O.; Elliott, A.; Bayat, M.
after.abstract: Purpose. To develop a data-efficient, clinically guided transfer-learning framework for hyperacute neurological outcome prediction from head CT in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) after cardiac arrest by leveraging free-text radiology report. Methods. This retrospective study included 683 patients with available CT examination and radiology reports from December 2015 to November 2025. The primary outcome distinguished favorable neurological outcomes (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) from neurological death due to brain death or cerebral herniation (CPC 5). A cross-attention adaptor jointly learned to predict neurological outcome and five report-derived manifestations of brain injury from a frozen pretrained head CT encoder. Outcome prediction used CT images alone at inference. The manifestation-guided adaptor, trained with and without additional patients who contributed only manifestation labels, was compared with outcome-only adaptor and two pooled-feature baselines. Performance was summarized as mean {+/-} SD across five held-out folds. Results. Of 683 patients, 197 were eligible for outcome evaluation (63 with favorable outcomes and 134 with neurological death), and 486 formed the manifestation-only cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.918 {+/-} 0.044 for the outcome-only adaptor. The manifestation-guided adaptor achieved an AUROC of 0.927 {+/-} 0.042. With additional manifestation-only training data, the adaptor achieved the mean AUROC (0.929 {+/-} 0.037), specificity (93.7% {+/-} 6.5%), with a sensitivity of 79.9% {+/-} 9.2%. Conclusion. Manifestation-guided adaptation outperforms outcome-only adaptation for neurological outcome prediction from hyperacute head CT after ECPR. Report-derived manifestation labels enabled training with additional examinations without eligible outcome labels while preserving CT-only prediction.
