after.authors: Yuh, E. L.; Jain, S.; Sun, X.; Rincon, S. P.; Mukherjee, P.; Yue, J. K.; Markowitz, A. J.; Mac Donald, C. L.; Satris, G. G.; Taylor, S. R.; Giacino, J. T.; McCrea, M. W.; Stein, M. B.; Temkin, N. R.; Diaz-Arrastia, R. R.; Robertson, C. S.; Okonkwo, D. O.; Manley, G. T.; TRACK-TBI Investigators,
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurological Surgery, University of California, San Francisco, CA
after.abstract: Importance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are commonly observed in mild TBI (mTBI). However, questions remain regarding their long-term prognostic significance. Objective: Determine whether traumatic microbleeds predict unfavorable outcome after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) Design: The prospective longitudinal observational Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury (TRACK-TBI) study enrolled acute TBI patients presenting to Emergency Departments (ED) at 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers between 2/26/2014-08/08/2018. CT and MRI were evaluated using the National Institutes of Health National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH NINDS) TBI Common Data Elements. Outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended (GOSE-TBI) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury. Setting: 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers Participants: 929 GCS 13-15 patients at least 17 years of age (38.5 +/- 16.5 years, 66% male) who underwent clinical head CT <24 hours after injury and brain MRI at 2 weeks post-injury and had at least one GOSE-TBI outcome score during 1 year follow-up. Exposure(s): Acute non-penetrating head trauma Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s): Frequency and co-occurrence of CT and MR features; incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. 8) and unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5 vs. >=5) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months Results: Generalized estimating equation models showed that TMBs and/or IVH were strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5 vs. >=5) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury, but not with incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8). For prediction of GOSE-TBI <5 vs. >=5 TMBs surpassed the importance of all demographic and baseline clinical predictors throughout the 1-year follow-up period. For prediction of incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8), brain contusions, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and subdural hematoma were more important throughout the 12-month follow-up period. Conclusions and Relevance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are common in mTBI. The presence of 4 or more TMBs and/or IVH is strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5) after mTBI out to at least 1 year, even after controlling for other neuroimaging abnormalities and demographic and clinical predictors. Better understanding of the implications of TMBs for long-term functional outcome may inform rehabilitation planning.

after.title: Preprint: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children
after.authors: Georgette, N.; Buckley, T.; Fine, A. M.; Jones, J.; McMurry, A. J.; Geanacopoulos, A.; Genadry, K. C.; Hoffmann, R.; Kahane, C.; Manrai, A. K.; Mandl, K. D.
after.abstract: Background Misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis of children in pediatric emergency departments lead to complications, and are particularly problematic in settings with limited pediatric expertise. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in diagnostic reasoning for adult emergency department patients, but utility for pediatric cases is largely untested. Methods Retrospective study of patients seen in the emergency department of a major urban pediatric academic medical center and subsequently admitted to the operating room or inpatient service. Records from 100 patients were randomly selected, stratified by age. We compared the accuracy of differential diagnoses (up to five, ranked by likelihood) generated by an LLM agent, Dr CaBot (one configuration with literature search, the other without), with those of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians (diagnosticians), all masked to outcome. Encounters were presented to diagnosticians stepwise across four touchpoints: triage, the initial physician evaluation (the a priori primary touchpoint), the full emergency department encounter, and the admission. Ground truth diagnosis was determined by two independent, board-certified pediatric emergency physicians (reviewers) based on the entire clinical encounter. The reviewers, masked to source, then assigned each differential a Bond score (0 to 5; 4 or above was high-scoring). Findings The median patient age was 4 years and 41% had a complex chronic condition. Bond score agreement between the two reviewers had a weighted kappa of 0.64. For the primary comparison at the initial physician evaluation touchpoint, the LLM agent and the diagnosticians both achieved high-scoring differentials in 95% of cases (difference 0%, 95%CI: -5.8, 5.8%). No differences were detected at the other touchpoints. Interpretation Dr CaBot and attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians showed similar performance in generating differential diagnoses from clinical documentation, suggesting potential as a diagnostic aid. Whether this performance improves care, particularly outside pediatric specialty centers, requires prospective evaluation.

after.title: Preprint: Under-perception of overweight, not genetic risk, tracks weight-loss goal-setting in a direct-to-consumer genetics cohort
after.authors: Mompeo-Masachs, O.; Grice, S. J.; West, N. R.
after.abstract: Services that rely on people to recognise their own weight and set their own goals may miss those who do not see themselves as overweight. We examined how adults perceive their weight, whether genetic risk of obesity, measured body size or early weight history explains who under-perceives it, and how perception relates to the weight-management goal they set, in a direct-to-consumer genetics cohort that includes people who have not sought care for their weight (FitnessGenes; N = 20,617). Although 61% of participants were overweight or obese by BMI, only 37% described themselves as such; among those overweight or obese by BMI, 64.0% placed themselves in a lighter category than their BMI indicated. Under-perception was more common in men than in women (73.5% vs 51.6%), in younger adults and at lower BMI, and a sex difference in the same direction, though smaller, was present when non-recognition of overweight was assessed against waist-to-height ratio rather than BMI. FTO rs9939609 behaved as an obesity risk variant (+0.46 kg/m2 BMI and OR 1.18 for recalled childhood obesity per risk allele) but did not predict under-perception at a given BMI (per-allele OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.92-1.03), and neither did MC4R rs17782313 nor a combined score. A recalled history of childhood obesity, by contrast, was associated with heavier self-perception at the same adult BMI (+10.0 percentage points). At the same BMI, participants who under-perceived their weight were about half as likely to set a weight-loss goal (26.8% vs 47.5%; OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.48-0.56); among those obese by BMI, 49% who recognised it chose weight loss, against 18% who did not. Genotype did not predict goal-setting beyond its effect on BMI. Men were less likely both to recognise overweight and, having recognised it, to choose weight loss. Genetic risk of obesity therefore identifies who is likely to be heavier but not who will recognise it, and self-perception marks a group, mainly men and those at lower BMI, whom self-directed weight-management services are likely to under-reach.

after.title: Preprint: Evaluation of a Study Advisory Group on the Facilitators and Barriers to Patient Engagement
after.authors: Leung, B.; Schmidt, K.; Ahmed, S.; Aghabayli, F.; Jannat, K.
after.abstract: The facilitators and barriers to patient engagement in an advisory group (AG) were evaluated. The AG was formed to provide the patient voice in the development of a pragmatic trial to study multinutrient treatment in children with ADHD. The AG consisted of patient partners (those with lived experience and caregivers) and healthcare professionals (those working with children with ADHD). Eleven AG members completed the Patient Engagement in Research Scale, and five members participated in semi-structured interviews. Qualitative data were analyzed thematically, and five themes were identified. Together with the quantitative findings, key facilitators of engagement included flexible engagement, a sense of trust among AG members and the research team, and meaningful opportunities to contribute. Barriers included irregular communication from the research team, ambiguity regarding members roles, and underutilization of members competencies. Findings highlight the importance of interpersonal relationships and team dynamics and informed improvements such as more regular communication, improved onboarding processes to strengthen role clarity, and better leveraging of members expertise to support full engagement. This evaluation provides insights into the use of research evaluation to strengthen patient engagement in applied research settings.

after.title: Preprint: Blood acceleration metric: A potential surrogate for fractional flow reserve to assess the functional severity of carotid artery stenosis
after.authors: Lovera, M. M.; Charitatos, V.; de Zelicourt, D.; Dubs, L.; Buoso, S.; Zipser, C. M.; Wegener, S.; Winklhofer, S.; Alkadhi, H.; Kurtcuoglu, V.
after.abstract: Purely morphological assessment of an arterial stenosis is not sufficient to adequately evaluate its functional significance. The metric of fractional flow reserve (FFR) is the gold standard for assessing coronary artery stenoses. However, the risks associated with catheterization and induction of hyperemia needed to measure FFR impede its application to cerebral vessels. Approaches based on a combination of computed tomography (CT) with computer simulations have been proposed to address this issue, yielding an estimate of fractional flow reserved (FFRCT). While promising, they are time-consuming and difficult to integrate into established clinical workflows. Here, we propose a new, easily derivable parameter termed the blood acceleration metric (BAM). It incorporates readily measurable morphological and hemodynamic features, such as minimum stenosis diameter and peak systolic velocity, to assess the functional severity of carotid artery stenoses. Preliminary assessment on 27 mild to moderate stenoses indicates a strong negative correlation (R=-0.85) between BAM and FFRCT. BAM should be further evaluated as a potential surrogate for FFR and, thereby, as a possible predictor of stroke risk.

after.title: Preprint: Previewing gaze behaviours predict gait speed, risky stepping strategies and cognitive dual task cost in older adults
after.authors: McVeigh-Mellor, O.; Cocks, A.; O'Reilly, L.; Orth, D.; Bruton, A.; Ellmers, T. J.; Kal, E.
after.abstract: Background: Previous work demonstrated that route previewing improves adaptive gait performance in older adults. However, it is unknown if specific gaze behaviours during previewing are associated with these benefits. Specifically, little is known about how older adults visually scan future walking routes during a given previewing period and whether different gaze behaviours are associated with subsequent walking performance. Methods: Gaze and gait data were collected from 29 older adults (Mage = 73.9, SD = 8.1 years; n = 19 female) during dual-task adaptive walking, preceded by a 10-second period in which they were instructed to preview their walking route. Eye-tracking measures across defined areas of interest during previewing and subsequent gait measures were analysed using linear and generalized mixed-effects models to determine whether previewing gaze behaviours predicted gait outcomes and cognitive dual-task cost. Results: Greater gaze sequence complexity (LZC_task) during previewing was associated with lower cognitive dual-task cost during walking, Larger gaze transition sizes predicted slower walking speed while greater duration of distal fixation allocation was associated with an increased likelihood of risky stepping behaviours. No previewing gaze behaviours predicted more than one gait outcome, and no significant relationships were observed between gaze behaviours and stepping errors. Conclusions: Different aspects of visual previewing were associated with distinct locomotor and cognitive outcomes. Greater gaze-sequence complexity was associated with lower cognitive dual-task cost. In contrast, larger gaze transitions predicted slower walking. Together, these findings suggest that effective previewing may depend on integrating proximal and distal route information into a coherent prospective stepping plan, rather than simply looking further ahead. Understanding how older adults visually plan upcoming routes may help inform approaches to reducing dual-task-related impairments in adaptive walking.

after.title: Preprint: Central motor cortical repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation at 5 Hz or 10 Hz combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation for ataxia in multiple system atrophy of the cerebellar type: a retrospective cohort study of efficacy and predictors of response
after.authors: Wang, M.; Wang, Y.; Wang, M.; Han, Y.; Pan, J.; Zhou, Y.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Sanbo Brain Hospital, Capital Medical University
after.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the efficacy of central motor cortical repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) at different frequencies (5 Hz and 10 Hz) combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation on the core domains of ataxia in patients with multiple system atrophy of the cerebellar type (MSA-C), and to explore the independent predictors of the response. Methods: In this retrospective study, 48 patients with a confirmed diagnosis of MSA-C were included. All patients received bilateral cerebellar hemispheric 1 Hz rTMS as background therapy and were divided according to the frequency of central cortical stimulation into a control group (cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation only, n=15), a 5 Hz combination group (n=16) and a 10 Hz combination group (n=17). Ataxia severity before and after treatment was assessed with the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS); absolute improvements and improvement rates were calculated for each subscore and for the total score. Continuous variables were described as mean +/- standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range) according to normality; within-group pre-post comparisons used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and between-group comparisons used one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis H test with Bonferroni correction. Clinical response was defined by an absolute improvement threshold (delta-ICARS total score >= 8 points), and independent influencing factors were analysed by Firth-penalised logistic regression; sensitivity analyses were performed with a total-score improvement rate >= 20% (and with >= 15% and >= 30% as alternative thresholds), and robustness results are reported for the delta-ICARS >= 10-point criterion. Missing cognitive and mood scale scores were imputed by multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; m=5; the mean of the five imputations constituted the analysis dataset) and then included in the analysis. Subgroup and interaction analyses were performed according to the median disease duration (2 years) and median age (57 years). Results: After treatment, the ICARS total score in the overall cohort was significantly lower than at baseline (median difference 7.0 points, P<0.001), and posture and gait (ICARS1), limb kinetic function (ICARS2) and speech function (ICARS3) all improved significantly (P<0.001 for all), whereas oculomotor disorders (ICARS4) did not improve significantly (P=0.799). Efficacy differed significantly among the three groups: median total-score improvement rates were 10.7%, 20.3% and 21.9%, respectively (P=0.004); when a total-score improvement rate >= 20% was used to define clinically significant efficacy, the response rates of the three groups were 6.7%, 50.0% and 58.8% (P=0.006), and both the 10 Hz and 5 Hz groups were significantly better than the control group (Bonferroni-corrected P=0.006 and P=0.040), with no statistically significant difference between the two frequencies. Domain-specific comparison showed statistically significant between-group differences in both the absolute improvement and the improvement rate of limb kinetic function (P=0.013 and P=0.005), with the 10 Hz group significantly better than the control group. When clinical response was defined as delta-ICARS >= 8 points, the response rates of the three groups were 20.0%, 56.2% and 64.7% (P=0.029); Firth-penalised multivariable regression showed that baseline ICARS total score was an independent predictor of clinical response (OR=1.076, 95% CI 1.013-1.143, P=0.017), whereas 5 Hz (OR=4.298, 95% CI 0.757-24.412, P=0.100) and 10 Hz (OR=5.847, 95% CI 0.885-38.640, P=0.067) stimulation did not reach independent statistical significance after adjustment. When response was defined as delta-ICARS >= 10 points, the response rates were 0%, 43.8% and 47.1% (P=0.007), and there were no responders in the control group. Subgroup analysis showed a significant group-by-age interaction (P=0.020); the clinical response rate of patients aged >= 57 years receiving 10 Hz stimulation was 85.7% (exploratory finding; small subgroup sample). The group-by-duration interaction was not statistically significant (P=0.210). Conclusions: Central 5 Hz and 10 Hz rTMS combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation both significantly improved the symptoms of ataxia in patients with MSA-C, and the efficacy was domain-specific, with the greatest improvement in the limb kinetic domain; sensitivity analyses across multiple criteria (delta-ICARS >= 8 points, improvement rate >= 20%, delta-ICARS >= 10 points) consistently supported the efficacy benefit of high-frequency stimulation in the same direction, but stimulation frequency did not reach independent predictive statistical significance after adjustment, and baseline ICARS total score was significantly associated with absolute improvement. Age may have a modifying effect on the efficacy of stimulation frequency (exploratory finding; small sample). This study provides preliminary support for the efficacy of the central 10 Hz combined with cerebellar 1 Hz regimen; the optimal stimulation parameters and independent predictors remain to be verified in larger prospective studies.

after.title: Preprint: Adverse Events and Baseline Psychological Distress Among Dementia Family Care Partners in the Tele-STELLA Study
after.authors: McClure, C.; Chatterton, H.; Franklin, H.; Mooney, A.; Lindauer, A.
after.abstract: Background: Adverse event (AE) narratives may reveal physical and psychological challenges experienced by family care partners of people living with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Objective: To characterize care partner AEs during the national Tele-STELLA study and explore differences in baseline psychological characteristics by AE category and subcategory. Methods: This descriptive, exploratory analysis included 43 AEs reported by 36 care partners. Narratives were classified as Physical, Psychological, or Random/Other. Baseline depressive symptoms, grief, and behavioral reactivity were compared between care partners with and without each AE type within this sample. Results: Physcial events accounted for 48.8% of AEs, Psychological events for 39.5%, and Random/Other events for 11.6%. Infections predominated among Physical events; stress/distress accounted for half of the Psychological events. Psychological AEs were associated with higher baseline grief and behavioral reactivity. Stress/distress-related AEs were associated with higher depressive symptoms and reactivity, whereas aggression-related Aes were associated with greater grief. Conclusions: Care partner AE narratives captured heterogeneous physical and psychological experiences. Classification may complement conventional assessments of care partner health and distress. These exploratory findings do not establish causality or predictive validity and warrant prospective study.

after.title: Preprint: Evaluating the Clinical Utility of a Brief Remote Speech Assessment for Screening and Triage of Speech Disorders
after.authors: Dickerson, N. V.; Utianski, R. L.; Duffy, J. R.; Clark, H. M.; Stierwalt, J. A. G.; Barnard, L. R.; Staff, N. P.; Botha, H.
after.abstract: Purpose: Speech abnormalities can often be early or clinically important manifestations of neurologic disease, yet access to clinicians with specialized expertise required for comprehensive motor speech evaluation may limit timely assessment. Brief remote speech assessment could provide a scalable approach for identifying patients who warrant more comprehensive evaluation, but its utility across heterogeneous speech presentations remains unclear. This study evaluated the validity and clinical utility of the Mayo Speech Test (MST), a brief (~5-minute) audio-recorded remote speech assessment, relative to a comprehensive in-person motor speech examination (~1-hour). Specifically, we examined whether MST could support clinically meaningful screening and triage decisions by distinguishing normal from abnormal speech and identifying the presence of a speech disorder. Method: One hundred participants completed a comprehensive in-person speech evaluation and a remote MST. Participants were excluded when the interval between assessments exceeded 90 days (n = 13) or either rater judged audio quality insufficient for diagnostic interpretation (n = 6), with overlapping exclusions resulting in a final analytic sample of 82 participants. Remote recordings were independently evaluated by two speech-language pathologists (SLPs) who were blinded to participant identity. In-person evaluation classifications served as the clinical reference standard and were grouped as normal (n = 33), dysphonia only (n = 5), or speech disorder (n = 43). One participant could not be classified. Performance was evaluated for two clinically motivated binary decisions: distinguishing normal from abnormal (such as dysphonia or speech disorder; Tier 0) and identifying normal speech or dysphonia only versus speech disorder (Tier 1). Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, agreement, and error patterns were examined. Results: Both remote raters demonstrated similar overall performance despite differing error profiles. For Tier 0 screening, Rater 1 demonstrated 93.6% sensitivity and 71.9% specificity for identifying abnormal voice/speech, whereas Rater 2 demonstrated 78.7% sensitivity and 93.9% specificity. For Tier 1 identification of speech disorder, sensitivity and specificity were 83.3% and 86.5%, respectively, for Rater 1 and 71.4% and 97.4% for Rater 2. Interrater agreement was 79.7% for Tier 0 ({kappa} = 0.60) and 86.1% for Tier 1 ({kappa} = 0.72). Missed speech disorders represented an important source of error, with differences between raters indicating distinct thresholds for assigning abnormality and speech-disorder classifications. Conclusions: A brief remote speech assessment showed promising performance for broad clinical classification, particularly when used to address screening and triage questions rather than reproduce the diagnostic granularity of a comprehensive examination. Similar overall performance across raters masked meaningful sensitivity-specificity tradeoffs, highlighting the importance of examining error profiles in addition to aggregate accuracy. MST may therefore have clinical utility for identifying patients who warrant comprehensive motor speech evaluation, but should not be considered a substitute for a full diagnostic assessment.

after.abstract: Background: Variability in low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C) response to popular diets is well documented, but the factors contributing to this variability remain unclear. We examined whether genetic predisposition to high LDL-C impacts the effects of healthy low-carbohydrate (HLC) or healthy low-fat (HLF) diets on LDL-C. Methods: The Diet Intervention Examining the Factors Interacting with Treatment Success (DIETFITS) trial randomized 609 adults (ages 18-50 years; body mass index 28-40 kg/m2; not on lipid-lowering therapy) to a HLC or HLF diet for 12 months. This secondary analysis included 431 genotyped participants (HLC, n=223; HLF, n=208) with 24-hour recall and LDL-C data at baseline and 6 months. The primary exposure was a genome-wide polygenic score for LDL-C (PGS-LDL). The outcomes were 6-month change in LDL-C, LDL-C increase versus decrease, and new-onset hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C [≤] 130 mg/dL). Associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic and linear regression adjusted for baseline LDL-C, weight change, and other factors. Results: Mean baseline LDL-C was 116 mg/dL (SD, 26.1) in the HLC group and 111 mg/dL (SD, 30.6) in the HLF group. Similar effects on LDL-C lowering were not seen for HLF. In both, change in saturated fat intake was associated with change in LDL-C, independent of PGS-LDL, but this association was modified by PGS-LDL only in the HLC arm (P for interaction <0.0001). after.title: Preprint: Earlier confirmation of glaucoma progression with risk-weighted visual field and OCT scheduling
after.authors: Chen, L.; Fujita, A.; Moradi, M.; Eslami, M.; Elze, T.; Zebardast, N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Massachusetts Eye and Ear, Harvard Medical School
after.abstract: Glaucoma is monitored with visual field (VF) tests of function and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of structure, but models that predict progression do not determine when each test should be repeated. Here we present GEAR (gated expected-delay allocation rule), a policy that pairs a longitudinal risk predictor with a decision layer and gives each eye separate VF and OCT intervals. In the decision layer, clinical gates define the admissible test intervals, and an explicit objective selects the intervals that minimize risk-weighted detection delay plus a penalty on expected testing, with penalties fixed to a routine-testing budget. In retrospective replay of held-out records (5,935 visits from 1,681 patients), GEAR with risk-based confirmation timing confirmed simulated progression 3.4 months earlier than annual VF and OCT testing (95% confidence interval, 2.7-4.1) at a comparable testing rate. The reduction persisted against a guideline-informed comparator and a reconstructed Kalman comparator, under an alternative onset assumption and with a VF-only adaptation in an external dataset.

after.title: Preprint: The vertical velocity step test and vertical sinusoidal harmonic acceleration test
after.authors: Mochizuki, F.; Williams, E.; Hawthorne, M.; Miro, B.; Kiderman, A.; Hoffer, M. E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Miami Miller School of Medicine
after.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Current rotational chair testing assesses only horizontal semicircular canal (SCC) function. This study characterizes vertical SCC responses and provides preliminary descriptive reference ranges using sinusoidal harmonic acceleration (vSHA) and velocity step (vVST) paradigms. METHODS: Forty-one healthy adults were tested with an adapted rotational chair to position the left anterior-right posterior (LARP) and right anterior-left posterior (RALP) SCCs in the Earth-horizontal plane. vSHA (at 0.08, 0.16, and 0.64 Hz) and vVST (at 100/s) were performed. Gain, phase, asymmetry, time constants (TC), and maximum slow-phase eye velocity (MSPEV) were compared across planes. Correlations with video head impulse test (vHIT) gain were also examined. RESULTS: vSHA gain (LARP: 0.37-0.43; RALP: 0.38-0.42) was lower than horizontal gain (0.59-0.63), consistent with previously reported vertical canal measurements. Cross-plane Friedman tests confirmed significantly lower vertical than horizontal gain at all three frequencies (all p < .001). Vertical phase lead exceeded horizontal at 0.08 and 0.16 Hz (all p-adjusted [≤] .021). Vertical TC were significantly shorter than horizontal for both per- and post-rotation (all p-adjusted < .001), and per- and post-rotation TC did not differ significantly in any plane. No significant LARP-RALP differences or vHIT-vVST correlations were found. CONCLUSIONS: vSHA and vVST characterize vertical SCC function non-redundantly with horizontal testing and vHIT. In the vertical planes, gain values and TCs were reduced, which represents a pattern consistent with reduced velocity storage. Validation in larger and clinical samples is required before clinical adoption.

after.title: Preprint: Transparent Implementation and Benchmarking of ACMG/AMP Variant Classification in fastVEP
after.authors: Huang, K.-l.; Ganapathi, M.; Chung, W.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
after.abstract: Background: The ACMG/AMP framework is the standard for germline sequence variant interpretation, but applying it in scalable automated software requires operational choices that the original framework and later ClinGen guidance do not always specify. We implemented an ACMG/AMP classification engine within fastVEP and evaluated which implementation choices improved agreement with expert-curated classifications without increasing concerning opposite-direction calls. Methods: The classifier implements all 28 ACMG/AMP criteria and can evaluate 15 from a sites-only VCF using nine public evidence sources. For selecting the optimal classifier, we compared symmetric and hybrid evidence-combining schemes, pathogenic class cutoffs, population-frequency thresholds, and benign-evidence thresholds against 673,660 ClinVar variants with review status of two stars or higher from April 2026. Clinical geneticists reviewed opposite-direction calls. We then applied the selected final classifier unchanged to 116,078 variants that newly reached the two-star threshold in the October 2026 ClinVar release. Results: The final fastVEP ACMG/AMP classifier uses the Tavtigian point scale on the pathogenic side and the 2015 ACMG/AMP combining table on the benign side. Using the 2015 table on both sides reduced pathogenic-side recall from 62.5 to 57.1 percent and lost 4,900 same-direction calls while avoiding 10 opposite-direction pathogenic calls. Using points on both sides increased benign-side recall from 66.4 to 77.0 percent, but increased opposite-direction benign calls from 27 to 399 and reduced recall of ClinVar uncertain variants from 97.1 to 69.5 percent. The 6-point Likely pathogenic cutoff was retained because lowering it to 5 points increased pathogenic-side recall to 73.9 percent but also classified 6,003 additional ClinVar uncertain variants and 17 additional ClinVar benign-side variants as pathogenic-side. The final classifier reproduced ClinVar's exact five-tier class for 431,727 variants or 64.1 percent and its pathogenic, benign, or uncertain direction for 534,335 variants or 79.3 percent. Only 51 calls or 0.0076 percent were opposite in direction to ClinVar. On the later variants, same-direction agreement was 72.6 percent and 20 calls were opposite in direction. Conclusions: The rules used to combine evidence affected classification more than several individual numeric thresholds. The hybrid scheme increased pathogenic-side recall while preventing a single Supporting benign criterion from producing a directional call. This conservative operating profile is suited to large-scale variant triage because it makes high-confidence calls while leaving variants uncertain when the available evidence does not support expert-level resolution. fastVEP is a research and decision-support tool and does not replace case-specific expert review.

after.authors: Gandasegui, J.; Fleitas, P.; Messa, A.; Gelaye, W.; Shao, Y.; Degarege, D.; Bedane, D.; Novela, V.; de Jesus, A.; Dias, J.; Ambridge, K.; Sevilleno, N.; Bewsher, A.; K. Judah, T.; Mandomando, I.; Enbiale, W.; Lawley, T.; Krolewiecki, A.; Munoz, J.; Doyle, S. R.
after.abstract: Soil-transmitted helminth control relies on mass anthelmintic treatment, yet helminth-anthelmintic-microbiome interactions and their role on treatment response remain poorly understood. We characterised the microbiome, resistome, and functional profiles of 858 paired stool metagenomes from 429 children treated with albendazole or a fixed-dose albendazole-ivermectin co-formulation in the ALIVE clinical trial in Ethiopia and Mozambique. Baseline microbiome composition differed more by country than infection status and was not associated with albendazole efficacy or adverse events. Co-formulation treatment, particularly three consecutive daily doses, was associated with depletion of Enterobacteriaceae, predominantly Escherichia coli, in Ethiopia, with reductions in E. coli-associated resistance genes and metabolic pathways. Genome-resolved analyses of over 22,000 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes confirmed this depletion across multiple E. coli strain-level populations, linking taxonomic, resistome, and functional signals to one ecological event. These findings reveal an off-target effect of combination anthelmintic treatment relevant to large-scale deworming programmes and expand genomic resources for African gut microbiota.

after.authors: Jaganath, D.; Ainebyona, A.; Luiz, J.; Poore, H.; Banze, D.; Castro, R.; Yerlikaya, S.; Nahid, P.; Denkinger, C.; Adithya, C.; Khosa, C.; Zar, H. J.; Bhatt, N.; Wobudeya, E.

after.abstract: Background: Swab-based molecular testing for tuberculosis (TB) could provide a near point-of-care (nPOC) diagnostic for children. We evaluated the accuracy of two swab-based nPOC platforms to detect pediatric pulmonary TB. Methods: We prospectively enrolled children under 15 years with presumptive TB in Uganda and South Africa. They completed TB evaluation including sputum molecular testing and culture. Two tongue swabs were collected and tested with MiniDock MTB (Pluslife Biotech, China) and Truenat MTB Ultima (Molbio Diagnostics, India), and one swab was dipped in sputum for testing with MiniDock MTB. We calculated the sensitivity and specificity of each index test against a culture-based standard and compared them with sputum molecular testing and smear microscopy. Findings: We included 335 children, among whom median age was 3 years (IQR 1-6), 53% were female, 11% were living with HIV, and 16% had microbiologically confirmed TB. Tongue swabs were collected in all children, with invalid test rates of less than 3%. Against a culture-based standard, the sensitivities of tongue swab MiniDock MTB and MTB Ultima were 50% (95% CI 33.4-66.6) and 50% (95% CI 28.2-71.8), respectively, and specificities were [≥]98% for both. Sputum swab MiniDock MTB had similar sensitivity to sputum Xpert Ultra (85.7% vs. 75.0%, p=0.45), but substantially higher sensitivity than tongue swab MiniDock MTB (+23.1%, p=0.03) and sputum smear microscopy (+46.4%, p<0.001). Interpretation: Sputum swab testing had similar accuracy to sputum Xpert Ultra in children. Tongue swab testing had moderate accuracy, and has value to identify microbiologically confirmed cases when sputum is not available.

after.authors: Eilersen, A.; Poder, S.; Goedknegt, M. J. F.; Pedersen, A. G.; Ploug, J. B.; Davenport, R. J.; Simonsen, L.
after.abstract: Background. Historically, the Variola virus caused deadly smallpox epidemics in children. In Copenhagen, transmission was halted by 1810 when ~90% of children were vaccinated following the introduction of a mandatory single-dose vaccine program. A 14-year honeymoon period followed, but in 1824 smallpox re-emerged as a milder disease of adults. We set out to study smallpox epidemics between 1824 and 1835 when all smallpox patients in Copenhagen were quarantined. Methods. We analyze data from 3795 smallpox patients reported by the treating physicians between 1824 and 1835. The data include age, vaccination status, and outcome. We estimate age-specific case fatality ratios (CFR) and vaccine effectiveness (VE) against mortality. Findings. For the four outbreaks while quarantine was mandatory (1824-1834), the CFR was ~1% among the vaccinated and ~25% among the unvaccinated, corresponding to a VE of ~95%. For the fifth outbreak in 1835, we found that CFR was low among the vaccinated but increased with age, which is evidence of waning vaccine protection. Almost no cases were over 40 years of age, suggesting lifelong immunity from smallpox infection. Interpretation. As the unvaccinated CFR was high and comparable to the pre-vaccine era, the milder post-honeymoon smallpox disease cannot be explained by genetic changes in the virus. Rather, high coverage with an effective vaccine combined with waning vaccine protection in adulthood explains the changing face of smallpox. We demonstrates how high vaccine coverage can disguise an outbreak of highly pathogenic smallpox as the milder Variola minor. Funding This study was funded by the Danish National Research Foundation (grant no. DNRF170).

after.title: Preprint: An Interpretable DSP Architecture for ECG Rhythm and Premature Ventricular Contraction Detection in MATLAB/Simulink
after.authors: Atif, A.; Ferdous, M. J.
after.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring requires reliable signal preprocessing and interpretable detection of abnormal cardiac activity while maintaining low algorithmic complexity. This study presents an integrated digital signal processing architecture developed in MATLAB/Simulink for ECG preprocessing, QRS and R-peak detection, heart-rate estimation, rhythm classification, and premature ventricular contraction (PVC) detection. Real ECG recordings from the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database were used for development and evaluation. The preprocessing stage employs minimum-order elliptic IIR high-pass and low-pass filtering, followed by differentiation, squaring, moving-window integration, thresholding, and R-peak detection. RR intervals derived from detected R peaks are used for instantaneous heart-rate calculation and classification of normal rhythm, bradycardia, and tachycardia. PVC detection uses two interpretable beat-level features, an RR-interval ratio and a QRS-energy ratio, combined through fixed rule-based logic. Three initial 10-s windows containing 18 annotated PVCs were used during algorithm development and threshold selection. After the detector parameters were frozen, evaluation was performed on nine additional non-overlapping 10-s windows containing 56 expert-annotated PVCs from MIT-BIH Records 106, 119, and 200. Using a +/-100 ms event-matching tolerance, the held-out evaluation produced 40 true positives, 9 false positives, and 16 false negatives, corresponding to 71.43% sensitivity, 81.63% precision, and 76.19% F1 score. Across the same nine windows, the R-peak detector achieved 94.39% sensitivity, 99.02% positive predictivity, 96.65% F1 score, and approximately 16.91 ms mean absolute timing error. The results demonstrate the feasibility and limitations of a lightweight and explainable streaming ECG-processing architecture and motivate future work incorporating adaptive decision thresholds and broader patient-independent validation.

after.authors: Zuckerman, B. P.; Zangas, P.; Zhang, L.; Osadcha, A.; Zhao, S.; Georgakis, M. K.
after.abstract: Background: The inhibition of NOD-, LRR- and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome is an emerging therapeutic strategy for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Although early clinical trials demonstrate reductions in inflammatory biomarkers, whether these translate into cardiovascular benefit remains uncertain. We investigated the potential efficacy and safety of NLRP3 inhibition using human genetics. Methods: We developed a cis-genetic instrument for NLRP3 downregulation using C-reactive protein (CRP) associated variants (P<5 x 10^-8) within the NLRP3 locus (+/-100 kb of NLRP3 transcription start site) from 575,531 participants. Mendelian Randomization and colocalization analyses assessed the effect of the genetic instrument against gene expression of NLRP3 and other inflammatory mediators in immune cells, downstream inflammatory biomarkers, and pharmacodynamic responses to the NLRP3 inhibitor ruvonoflast. Two-sample Mendelian randomization assessed cardiovascular, cardiometabolic, and infectious outcomes, followed by phenome-wide analyses of 1,387 clinical outcomes. Results: Using 14 variants in the NLRP3 locus, we constructed a genetic instrument that corresponded to a 19% difference in circulating CRP between the extreme percentiles of its distribution. Colocalisation evidence suggested the effects on CRP to be driven by reduced NLRP3 expression in naive monocytes (PP.H4=98.7%). In accordance with the expected biological role of NLRP3, genetically proxied NLRP3 downregulation by the constructed instrument was associated with lower IL-18 (beta=-0.11; 95%CI, -0.14 to -0.08) and IL-6 (beta=-0.15; 95%CI, -0.17 to -0.12) and broadly similar pharmacodynamic effects to the NLRP3 inhibitor ruvonoflast across 8 biomarkers. Genetically proxied NLRP3 inhibition was associated with lower risk of recurrent pericarditis (OR per 19% decrease in CRP, 0.68, 95%CI, 0.58-0.80), but slightly elevated risk of coronary artery disease (OR, 1.06; 95%CI, 1.03-1.08) and peripheral arterial disease (OR, 1.10; 95%CI, 1.04-1.15) and no effect on ischaemic stroke (OR, 0.98; 95%CI, 0.94-1.02). The instrument was also associated with higher carotid-intima-media thickness and a worse cardiometabolic profile with increasing effects on blood pressure, waist-to-hip ratio, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides. We found no associations with increased risk for prespecified infectious disease outcomes. Conclusions: A genetic proxy for NLRP3 inflammasome downregulation reproduced key molecular effects of pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition but was not associated with reduced ASCVD risk.

after.authors: ALIZADEH, E.; Tamaki, J.; Moslemi, A.; Tachiki, T.; Sato, Y.; Hamada, M.; Tsuda, K.; Kudo, A.; Kamiya, K.; Imai, N.; Nitta, A.; Ohara, K.; Takashima, N.; Kitagawa, J.; Kouda, K.; Morita, A.; Uenishi, K.; Kajita, E.; Kagamimori, S.; Humbert, L.; Noailly, J.; Iki, M.
after.abstract: ABSTRACT Summary Hip fractures are among the most serious consequences of osteoporosis, yet many individuals who sustain hip fractures do not meet the diagnostic threshold based on areal bone mineral density (aBMD). Finite element (FE)-based mechanical descriptors may improve hip fracture prediction beyond aBMD. Purpose This study investigated whether FE-based mechanical descriptors derived from dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) improve hip fracture discrimination beyond aBMD in the Japanese Population-Based Osteoporosis (JPOS) cohort. Methods The study included 1,636 women, of whom 85 sustained hip fractures during 20 years of follow-up. Subject-specific three-dimensional femoral models were reconstructed from DXA images using statistical shape and appearance modelling, and nonlinear FE analyses were performed to derive mechanical descriptors under simulated sideways-fall loading. Predictive performance was evaluated using discrimination, model fit, reclassification, and hazard ratio analyses. Results Over two-thirds of women who experienced hip fracture were not classified as osteoporotic based on aBMD. Several FE-based descriptors significantly improved fracture prediction relative to total hip and femoral neck aBMD across the evaluation frameworks. The best-performing descriptor, combining femoral strength with residual energy (F_U + W_R), achieved a significantly higher AUROC of 0.797 compared with 0.763 (p = 0.026) and 0.757 (p = 0.040) for total hip and femoral neck aBMD, respectively, and the highest hazard ratio (3.577 per SD). The same descriptors consistently performed best across all evaluation methods. Conclusion These findings demonstrate that FE-based descriptors provide meaningful information beyond aBMD and may improve identification of women at elevated hip fracture risk.

after.title: Preprint: SARS-CoV-2 antibody landscape following multiple vaccinations and infections during Omicron period
after.authors: Yang, Y.; Juntila-Raymond, C.; Callear, A.; Smith, M.; Godonou, E.-T.; Monto, A. S.; Martin, E. T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Epidemiology, University of Michigan School of Public Health, Ann Arbor, MI, USA
after.abstract: Background: Repeated COVID-19 vaccination effects on the immunogenicity, breadth, and durability of antibody responses across antigenically distinct SARS-CoV-2 variants remain incompletely understood. Method: Participants receiving >= five COVID-19 vaccine doses 2020-2025 were selected from a prospective cohort in Michigan. Serum IgG, IgM, and ACE2 percent inhibition were measured using multiplex assays. Baseline-adjusted immunogenicity, cross-reactivity, and formulation-specific antibody durability were evaluated using regression models. Result: Twenty-one participants were included (median: seven vaccine doses). For every two-fold increase in pre-vaccination IgG concentration, post-vaccination fold-rise was 34% (95% CI: 16%-48%), 43% (95% CI: 15%-62%), and 55% (95% CI: 21%-75%) lower following monovalent, bivalent, and 2023-24 vaccination, while baseline-adjusted immunogenicity showed no significant trends across successive vaccines. Antibody landscapes demonstrated broad cross-reactivity against ancestral and Omicron variants, with similar strain-specific IgG changes across ancestral, vaccine-matched, and antigenically distant strains, but greater heterogeneity in ACE2 inhibition. Formulation-specific waning models showed significant IgG declines following monovalent and bivalent vaccination (beta = -1.03, 95% CI: -1.51 to -0.55; P<0.001 and -1.00 , 95% CI: -1.71 to -0.30; P=0.007, respectively) and ACE2 inhibition declines following monovalent vaccination, while other formulations showed less consistent changes. Despite waning, antibody levels generally remained relatively high across variants up to 300 days post-vaccination, with formulation-specific differences in durability. Conclusion: Repeated COVID-19 vaccination maintained baseline-adjusted immunogenicity and broad cross-reactive antibody responses, with formulation-specific differences in durability. Higher baseline immunity was associated with smaller post-vaccination increases, suggesting repeated boosting continues to reinforce humoral immunity despite increasingly complex immune histories.

after.authors: Menkir, T.; Roa-Contreras, J.; Peralta, Y.; Taylor, C.; McMahon, M.; Yeh, J.; Constanza Camargo, M.; Huang, R.; Ladabaum, U.; Alarid-Escudero, F.
after.abstract: Background Helicobacter pylori is the main cause of non-cardia gastric cancer. In the U.S. H. pylori seroprevalence has declined. However, whether all subgroups have benefited equally from this change is unclear. Further, prevalence alone cannot indicate when infection risk is most acute and thus when to target prevention efforts like screening. Methods We synthesized age-stratified H. pylori seroprevalence data from 36 U.S. studies (N=56,845; 1965-2014), identified via literature search through September 2022. We fitted Bayesian hierarchical catalytic epidemic models to estimate, by race/ethnicity (for each of five race/ethnicity groups) and birth cohort (pre-1960 vs. 1960+, or continuous), the maximum proportion infected, age-specific force of infection (FOI), and the age at half-maximum seroprevalence. Findings Disparities in maximum prevalence worsened in the 1960+ birth cohort, with the absolute Hispanic-Non-Hispanic White (NHW) gap widening from 33.2 to 51.4 percentage points. FOIs peaked at the youngest ages for the Non-Hispanic American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN) and Non-Hispanic Black (NHB) populations. Age patterns varied independently of burden; Hispanic and AI/AN populations reached similar peak prevalence (83.0% vs 76.1%) for the 1960+ birth cohort, yet the age at half-maximum seroprevalence was 19.3 years (95%CrI: 14.9, 23.5) vs 3.20 years (95%CrI: 1.99, 4.63). Continuous birth-cohort analyses supported these findings. Interpretation National declines in H. pylori mask widening racial and ethnic disparities. In AI/AN and NHB populations, seroprevalence rises steeply in early childhood, well before adulthood-targeted screen-and-treat programs would intervene. Moreover, similar peak prevalence can mask different age patterns of infection, and should be accounted for when guiding prevention strategies. Funding National Cancer Institute U01CA265729 and U01CA319219

after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Medical Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden
after.abstract: Background: Reliable assessment of avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) in young people may require information from both children and caregivers, yet cross-informant agreement has not been examined for the Pica, ARFID, and Rumination Disorder Interview (PARDI). This study evaluated agreement between child and parent PARDI interviews for ARFID diagnosis, individual DSM-5 Criterion A, ARFID dimensions, and overall severity. Methods: Twenty children aged 11-14 years screening positive for ARFID and one parent per child were recruited from the ARFID InitiativE Sweden (ARIES) cohort. Children and parents completed separate PARDI interviews with trained interviewers. Parent-child agreement was assessed using percentage agreement and Cohens kappa ({kappa}) for categorical ratings of ARFID diagnosis and Criterion A consequences. For continuous ratings of ARFID dimensions and overall severity, agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and paired t-tests comparing mean parent and child scores. Results: Parents gave higher mean scores than children across all continuous domains, although the difference was statistically significant only for overall severity (raw mean difference=0.42, p=.003). Parent-child agreement was poor for sensory sensitivity (ICC=0.42), moderate for lack of interest (ICC=0.63) and overall severity (ICC=0.71), and excellent for concern about aversive consequences (ICC=0.95). ARFID was identified in 17/20 parent interviews and 14/20 child interviews; diagnostic agreement was 75% ({kappa}=0.31, p=.133). Agreement was perfect (100%) for Criterion A1, high for A2 and A3 (both 95%), and lowest for psychosocial impairment (A4; 65% agreement, {kappa}=0.19). Item-level findings indicated a general tendency toward higher parental ratings, although children provided higher ratings on selected items involving food restriction, sensory experiences, hunger cues, and abdominal pain. Conclusions: Child and parent PARDI interviews provided overlapping but non-interchangeable information. Agreement varied across different aspects of ARFID, with greater discrepancies for psychosocial impairment and sensory sensitivity. These differences may partly reflect what children and parents are able to observe or experience directly. Multi-informant assessment may therefore offer a more complete account of pediatric ARFID than either response alone.

after.authors: Kegne, B. A.; Merhatsedk, D. M.; Mohammed, B. Y.; Taye, E. A.; Belay, S. A.
after.abstract: Abstract Background: Missed maternal postnatal assessment before discharge after facility birth is an undermeasured indicator of intrafacility quality of care that previous Ethiopian studies did not isolate in nationally representative analyses. This gap matters because women may reach facilities for childbirth yet leave without a basic maternal clinical assessment during the highest-risk postpartum period, making missed assessment a marker of effective coverage failure rather than conventional postnatal care utilization alone. Methods: We analyzed nationally representative 2024-2025 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey data for 3,645 women aged 15-49 years whose most recent live birth occurred in a health facility. All analyses incorporated sampling weights and survey design features. Factors associated with missed maternal postnatal assessment before discharge were examined using multilevel mixed-effects logistic regression accounting for clustering within enumeration areas, with adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) reported. Results: Overall, 40.1% (95% CI: 37.0-43.3) of women who delivered in Ethiopian health facilities did not receive a maternal postnatal assessment before discharge. after.title: Preprint: The plateau in liver disease mortality in Germany: contrasting trends by age, region and ICD-10 code, 2000-2024
after.authors: Kumpf, M.; Stambollxhiu, E.; Wende, E.; Lenhart, N.; Graf, M.; Ziegelmayer, S.; Makowski, M.; Bressem, K.; Adams, L.
after.abstract: Background: Cirrhosis is often diagnosed only at decompensation, making identification of high-risk groups important for prevention and early detection. Chronic liver disease mortality has fallen in southern Europe and France since 2010, but not in Germany. Whether the German plateau reflects birth-cohort alcohol exposure, metabolic liver disease or certification practice is unknown. Methods: Deaths by ICD-10 code, sex and age group were extracted from the WHO Mortality Database for 16 European countries (2000-2022), with Eurostat rates (2011-2023), German state-level mortality (1998-2024) and hospital diagnoses (2000-2023). Registry and Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2023 estimates were summarised for ages 45-64, 65-74 and 75 years and over, with registry rates standardised to the European Standard Population 2013. Findings: Germany's age-standardised chronic liver disease mortality was 16.6 per 100 000 in 2011 and 16.0 in 2023, against declines of 21-37% in France, Italy and Spain. Between 2010 and 2022, alcoholic liver disease mortality at ages 45-64 fell by 17% in men and 25% in women, whereas fibrosis and cirrhosis (K74) mortality at ages 65-74 rose by 27% and 28%, with larger K70-K77 mortality increases in eastern than western Germany. Hospitalisation rates showed similar age-specific patterns, while in-hospital case fatality declined. Fewer than 0.5% of liver deaths were certified as fatty liver. GBD 2023 showed a similar age-specific increase but attributed rising mortality to all five modelled aetiologies. Interpretation: The German plateau reflects continued decline below age 65 and rising mortality at ages 65-74, compatible with cohorts born 1945-59 reaching this age band, particularly in eastern Germany. Consumption records and surveys indicate differing regional patterns of alcohol exposure. Much of the cirrhosis in these cohorts is certified without aetiology, and GBD's aetiological estimates cannot be verified in registration data. Funding: None.

after.title: Preprint: A Whole-Blood Four-Gene Panel Distinguishes Pediatric Crohn's Disease from Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction
after.authors: Lunn, C.; Margolis, K.; Misirlioglu, P. K.; Xin, M.; Kapoor, V.; Afanasyeva, Y.; Albenberg, L.; Piccoli, D. A.; Okraku-Mantey, J.; Zapille, P.; Meyn, P.; Fenyo, D.; Levine, J.; Trasande, L.
after.abstract: Background and Aims: Crohn's disease and disorders of gut-brain interaction present with overlapping symptoms, and distinguishing them often requires endoscopy. We assessed whether the whole-blood transcriptome at presentation distinguishes these conditions and reflects disease activity. Methods: In a prospective two-center cohort, whole-blood RNA sequencing was performed in 425 treatment-naive participants aged 5 to 25 years (112 Crohn's disease, 313 disorders of gut-brain interaction). Differential expression was modeled for diagnosis and, within Crohn's disease, for the Pediatric Crohn's Disease Activity Index. Co-expression modules were integrated with protein-protein interaction networks, and machine learning distilled network genes into a diagnostic panel, evaluated internally and in an independent pediatric cohort. Results: Of 1,095 diagnosis-associated genes, 377 were also associated with disease activity, all with concordant direction. Five co-expression networks were perturbed, spanning neutrophil degranulation, hemostasis, interferon signaling, and T-cell and cytotoxic lymphocyte programs. A 4-gene panel (PSTPIP2, CLIC4, CACNB4, GZMK) drawn from 4 networks achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of up to 0.96 in held-out samples and up to 0.93 externally, with external specificity and positive predictive value of up to 0.95 and 0.93, respectively. The panel matched or exceeded every single-network panel with fewer genes, and minimally active Crohn's disease overlapped transcriptionally with disorders of gut-brain interaction. Conclusions: At diagnosis, Crohn's disease is distinguished from disorders of gut-brain interaction by a systemic signature of neutrophil and platelet activation and lymphocyte depletion that scales with disease activity. A 4-gene whole-blood panel may help prioritize symptomatic children for endoscopy and warrants prospective validation.

after.title: Preprint: High-resolution spatiotemporal estimates of total and wildfire PM2.5 in the contiguous United States, 2018-2024: Implications for population exposure and mortality burden
after.authors: Liu, N.; Cheong, Y.; Larson, T.; Austin, E.; Seto, E.
after.abstract:
Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

items.content_text: Heterogeneity in infectious disease spread reshapes the risk and severity of outbreaks. This heterogeneity can arise from intrinsic individual-level differences in susceptibility, contact patterns, and infectious durations. data.summary: added: Preprint: Emergent Heterogeneity in Compartmental Disease Models

after.title: Preprint: Emergent Heterogeneity in Compartmental Disease Models
after.authors: Roswell, M.; Aghaeeyan, A.; Goel, T.; Beckett, S. J.; Weitz, J. S.; Dushoff, J.
after.abstract: Heterogeneity in infectious disease spread reshapes the risk and severity of outbreaks. This heterogeneity can arise from intrinsic individual-level differences in susceptibility, contact patterns, and infectious durations. Heterogeneity can also emerge from disease dynamics in a canonically homogeneous population, due to the fact that individuals randomly become infected at different times, recover after different intervals, and have access to different numbers of susceptible individuals. Here, we explore the mechanisms generating emergent heterogeneity by analyzing secondary case distributions within the SIR model. We show numerically and prove analytically that the variation in secondary cases, calculated over the course of the epidemic, does not change with R0. This is in contrast to the increasing variation in secondary cases in the linearized SIR model, often used to study heterogeneity at the beginning of an outbreak. When we consider "forward cohorts" of individuals infected at the same time, between-cohort variation increases as R0 increases, while within-cohort variation decreases. We show that these effects balance exactly, leading to the invariance of the variation in secondary cases with respect to R0. These results demonstrate the importance of considering emergent, as well as intrinsic, variation between individuals and of considering heterogeneity of transmission spread over the whole epidemic cycle, including substantive dynamical effects that appear even in the initial outbreak phase.

Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

after.title: Preprint: Uncertainty-aware longitudinal prediction of multiple adverse pregnancy outcomes
after.authors: Wu, Y.; Asvadi, S.; van der Ven, M.; Peri, E.; Xu, M.; van der Hout-van der Jagt, M. B.; OEH van Laar, J.; Chen, C.; Luo, Q.; Mischi, M.; Oei, S. G.; Long, X.
after.abstract: Risk of pregnancy complications is reassessed at each antenatal visit, but whether earlier predictions add information beyond the most recent one is unclear. Classifying every prediction as low or high risk can leave uncertainty unexpressed. Whether reliability per visit holds across visits is also unclear. This secondary analysis included 9289 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort (eight US centres, 2010-2013). Logistic regression models predicted gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, suspected fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age at 6-13, 16-21 and 22-29 weeks (Visits 3). Mondrian conformal prediction reported 'no' (low risk), 'yes' (high risk), or both (review). To test whether prediction history adds information beyond the Visit 3 prediction, we compared, among women classified as high risk at Visit 3, those first classified as high risk at Visit 2 or 3 (emerging high) with those classified as high risk at all three visits (persistent high), adjusting for Visit 3 predicted probability. The adjusted proportion with the outcome was higher in the emerging-high than the persistent-high group, by 6.1 percentage points for large for gestational age (95% CI -0.4 to 12.2) and 3.8 percentage points for suspected fetal growth restriction (-0.9 to 8.1). Other outcomes showed adjusted differences close to zero. With conformal prediction calibrated to a 90% level at each visit, the reported answers included the actual outcome in 89.6-90.6% of women at each visit (coverage). Coverage decreased when each woman's three visits were considered together (79.0-85.4%). For fetal growth outcomes, how a woman's predicted risk evolved during pregnancy may add information beyond her Visit 3 prediction. For repeated clinical use, the target coverage level should reflect the acceptable risk of incorrect low- or high-risk classifications over a woman's follow-up and the clinical decisions supported at each visit.

after.title: Preprint: Microcirculation Mirror: A zero-install browser workstation for hand microvascular anatomy and nailfold capillaroscopy
after.authors: Wang, Y.; He, J.; Liu, W.; Xu, X.; Li, B.; Li, Y.; Wang, B.; Liu, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College
after.abstract: Background Hand microvasculature is conventionally presented through diagrams, cadaveric atlases and specialized optical instruments, while conventional clinical radiography cannot resolve individual capillary loops (5-15 m lumen) in vivo, which dominate cutaneous oxygen exchange. Methods We present Microcirculation Mirror, a zero-install browser workstation that registers layered hand anatomy to a live 21-landmark pose and couples it to a nailfold video capillaroscopy (NVC) simulator, a lumped microcirculatory model and an imaging-physics module. The single-file application runs offline on a laptop or, over local HTTPS, on a phone as an installable app. Results Its 3D atlas contains 136 named structures per hand in six systems from open Z-Anatomy/BodyParts3D meshes, plus a literature-parameterized capillary layer. The NVC module renders a 200x, 1.2-mm field with six deterministic patterns and quantified density, giant capillaries, avascular width fraction, hemorrhages, tortuosity and ramification. A lumped model reports nine estimates (SIM); a physics module shows that a 10-m capillary occupies 0.07 of a 150-m detector pixel; with iodinated contrast it retains {approx}0.016% effective contrast, about 60x below a 1% detection threshold; unenhanced blood is {approx}270x lower. The 2D stage renders in 2.9 ms per frame; system merging reduces atlas draw calls from 136 to 6. Conclusions The camera-overlay layers are templates, the atlas macro-anatomy is open mesh data, and the capillary layer is sampled. No patient data are used. The instrument is a product prototype, not a medical device, and provides a reproducible framework for making multi-scale microvascular reasoning visible.

after.title: Preprint: Requirements of a knowledge support tool for self-harm in general practice: a mixed-methods study with patients, carers, and clinicians
after.authors: Cant, H.; Mughal, F.; Asmal, S.; Petersen, K.; Groves, J.; Gardiner, E.; Bower, P.; Webb, R. T.; Kapur, N.; Westhead, J.; Palin, V.; Pate, A.; van Staa, T.; Quinlivan, L.
after.abstract: Background General practice has a central role in care following self-harm. However, clinicians frequently report uncertainty about best practice and patients describe poor care. A knowledge support tool is an add-on to electronic health systems that may improve services by providing personalised care information. Aim To understand what general practice clinicians, patients and carers need from a novel knowledge support tool for self-harm. Design and Setting Mixed-methods, using quantitative ratings, focus groups and follow-on interviews with general practice clinicians and patients/carers with lived experience of self-harm. Method Clinicians were recruited through social media and professional networks, and patients/carers through a third-sector organisation. During four focus groups and follow-on interviews, we explored the utility of potential content and functionality of a knowledge support tool. Quantitative utility ratings were summarised descriptively and qualitative data were analysed thematically using the framework method. People with lived/living experience were involved throughout. Results 13 clinicians and 14 patients/carers participated. Requirements of the knowledge support tool were captured across three qualitative themes: facilitating person-centred care, accessibility and usability, and balancing competing priorities of general practice. Across these themes, patients' and carers' needs were centred on promoting compassionate relationships and patient agency. Clinicians shared these needs but balanced them with a need to manage patient expectations and practice defensively under limited resources. Conclusion Our findings inform the core design of a knowledge support tool and suggest that such a tool could support the assessment and management of self-harm in general practice.

after.title: Preprint: Eye-to-Eye: Gaze detection as a proxy for medical doctor behaviour during virtual and in-person appointments
after.authors: Antao, R.; Moreno, P.; Santos-Victor, J.; da Silva, N. A.; Santos, R.; Leite, F.; Ferreira, D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Instituto Superior Tecnico - Universidade de Lisboa
after.abstract: The gaze direction of the physician during consultations plays an important role in patient satisfaction, with several studies pointing to the positive correlation between the amount of time the physician spends looking at the patient and patient satisfaction. Additionally, the effects of the virtual consultation environment on the gaze behaviour of the doctor have yet to be studied. Therefore, this study aims to assess the impact of the virtual consultation environment by comparing the amount of total time the doctor spends looking at the patient between face-to-face and virtual consultations, as well as the average duration during the consultation and the gaze frequency. The study population consisted of 14 doctors divided between 4 medical specialties: Gynaecology/Obstetrics (4), Neurology (3), Endocrinology (3) and General and Familiar Medicine (4). A low-cost desktop that runs an appearance-based gaze estimation pipeline was implemented in the clinical setup. Each doctor recorded 20 face-to-face consultations and 20 virtual consultations, which were then processed by the pipeline to obtain the percentage of time the doctor spent looking at the patient during the consultation. Overall, we found that doctors look more at the patient in virtual consultations compared to face-to-face consultations, both in total time and average duration during the consultation. Within medical specialties, three out the four specialties involved presented clear tendencies to look more at the patient in virtual consultations when compared to face-to-face consultations.

after.abstract: Abstract Background: Multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings are central to cancer care. National policy, including the 2026 National Cancer Plan for England, expects MDTs to improve how they work. after.title: Preprint: Uptake and outcomes of earlier viral load testing and longer visit intervals in the early HIV treatment period: retrospective cohort analysis of South Africas 2023 ART guidelines revision
after.authors: Kachingwe, E.; Maskew, M.; Mutanda, N.; Benade, M.; Scott, N.; Morgan, A.; Sande, L.; Ntjikelane, V.; Malala, L.; Manganyane, M.; Rosen, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: School of Public Health, Boston University, Boston, MA, USA
after.abstract: Background: South Africas 2023 revised ART Guidelines moved the first scheduled viral load (VL) test from 6 to 3 months after antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and accelerated differentiated care eligibility from 7 to 4 months among virally suppressed clients. We assessed uptake of these changes and their association with virologic outcomes. Methods: We analysed routine electronic medical record data from 18 primary healthcare clinics in three South African districts among all adults initiating or re-initiating ART (N=16,338; January 2022-March 2025). Interrupted time series analyses were used to assess uptake of 3-month VL testing and assignment to greater than or equal to 6-month visit intervals following guideline implementation in April 2023. Modified Poisson regression was used to compare relative risks (RRs) for viral suppression at the first and second routine VL tests among clients tested at 3 months (test window=56-111 days) and 6 months (112-<252 days). Results: At the first VL assessment, 27% of participants had VL tests at 3 months and 30% at 6 months; the rest had tests outside either window (19%) or no test documented (25%). Three-month VL testing rose immediately after guideline implementation, reaching 72-85% coverage by the end of the study period. Assignment to greater than or equal to 6month visit intervals among clients with 3-month viral suppression increased after implementation, reaching 48-71% across districts. A second VL result was documented for 62% of clients tested in the 3- or 6-month window. Viral suppression did not differ meaningfully between clients initially tested at 3 months (72%) and those initially tested at 6 months (72%). Among clients with a second scheduled VL result, 82% were virally suppressed. Assignment to greater than or equal to 6-month visit intervals was not associated with subsequent viral suppression (aRR 1.02, 95% CI 0.99-1.06). Results should be interpreted with caution due to missing VL data. Conclusion: South Africas 2023 guideline revision was associated with rapid increases in 3-month VL testing and assignment to longer visit intervals. Viral suppression at the first VL test was similar among clients tested at 3 and 6 months, and longer visit intervals were not associated with poorer outcomes. These findings support earlier differentiation of HIV care within routine service delivery. Incomplete uptake of recommended testing and visit intervals offers opportunities to strengthen implementation and warrants continued evaluation of longer-term outcomes.

after.title: Preprint: Practical evaluation of AI models to forecast a respiratory seasonal epidemic in Canada
after.authors: Benteke, B. L.; Yusuf, W.; Cojocaru, M. G.; Champredon, D.
after.abstract: Public health organizations can benefit greatly from infectious disease epidemic forecasting to guide and support interventions and policies that reduce morbidity. However, accurate and reliable epidemic forecasting remains notoriously challenging and is an evolving field in which new scientific advances continue to support forecasting efforts. Computational models that underpin artificial intelligence (AI) models are promising developments that may improve seasonal epidemic forecasting. This study aims to compare the performance of a selection of AI models previously identified as well adapted to epidemic forecasting, including machine learning (XGBoost), deep learning models (Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Transformer), time-series foundation model (Chronos), and a hybrid model: physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), against statistical models (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Prophet) and a compartmental epidemiological model (CEM) in seasonal epidemic forecasting across Canada. The study uses weekly positivity-rate incidence of seasonal influenza A across eight Canadian provinces during the 2025/2026 season as a test case. Each model generated short-term (up to 5 weeks ahead) forecasts independently for each province from October 11, 2025, to March 28, 2026. We evaluated performance using mean absolute error (MAE) for each province. Our results show that AI models, specifically GRU, Transformer, and Chronos models, achieve lower MAE than CEM in four of eight provinces (Alberta, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, and Saskatchewan). Meanwhile, CEM and ARIMA outperform all AI models in three provinces (Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba) and one province (Nova Scotia), respectively. Furthermore, data pooling strategies that leverage multi-province data for the target virus or multi-virus data within individual provinces greatly improve deep learning models, and Chronos performs well under zero-shot forecasting in British Columbia. In contrast, Prophet always has the highest MAE, and PINN is worse than CEMs. Overall, AI models performed comparably to, or slightly better than, CEMs. However, these modest gains may not offset their lack of interpretability, high computational costs, and reliance on the specialized expertise required for implementation. We therefore conclude that AI models are best as a complement, rather than a replacement, to CEMs, which remain crucial for interpretability and informing decision-making.

after.authors: Baldenweck, L.; Djisalov, M.; Pinamonti, D.; manzano, M.; Gadjanski, I.; Vidic, J.
after.abstract: An advanced LAMP assay targeting the mecA gene in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was developed and validated using clinical and foodborne S. aureus isolates. Reference strains, including both methicillin-sensitive and methicillin-resistant S. aureus, were used to evaluate and optimize assay performance. With the newly designed ID16 LAMP primer set, the detection limit for mecA was 15 fg/L of total genomic DNA, equivalent to 5 copies/L, and the assay turnaround time was only 25 min. All mecA-positive isolates identified by conventional qPCR were successfully detected by the LAMP assay. Overall, the developed LAMP method provides a rapid, highly specific, and sensitive alternative for mecA detection.
